div.head: PLEASANT PARAGRAPHS.
div.p: PLEASANT PARAGRAPHS.
IT is always best for a man to keep his temper.

No one else ;ants it. MANY a man who thinks himself ahead of the times is about as useless as a clock that runs too fast. A SHOEMAKERS TOAST—" May we have all the women in the country to shoe and all the men to boot !" BROKEN.—" I've had enough experience, and have concluded to stop betting for good and all." "I'll bet you five shillings you won't.'. "I'll take

you . A GENTLEMAN asked a minister: "When do you expect to see Deacon S. again?" "Never," said the minister, solemnly. "The deacon is in heaven. BOWERS says it is a wonder ther3 is any truth- fulness in the world, when mankind begins life by lying in the cradle. IN COURT.—Presiding Judge: "You have crushed a gentleman with your bicycle." De- fendant : " Quite true, Monsieur le President ; but put yourself in my place." Judge: " ; Wil- hut you, put yourself in his." HOLIDAY REVELLER: "Look here, I say; Hanged if there ain't a black hair in this soup !" IrAte Landlady: "Well, I'm sure! I suppose I ain't bound to keep a carroty haired cook just to please you, am I?' YOUNG WIFE (the week after the wedding) : "And now that supper is over, John, I don't mind you smoking your cigar in the house one bit, so sit down and. enjoy it quietly and comfortably." "What !" cried the husband, delightedly. "You don't object to my smoking? Good! I'll have to go to the club and let them all know what a kind, thoughtful angel of a wife I've got!" "AND how do your fowls lay, with the patent oil- stove in the hen-house?' Oh, they like it immensely, and lay well. Why, when I looked in last night, the ducks were sitting round it telling tales IF you are well-to-do, associate with the well-to- do for they are not likely to borrow ; but, if you are poor, keep on good terms with the poor, for they are more willing to lend. PLEASING VIE TEACHER. —Teacher : "Why was Solomon the wisest man in the world?" Boy: "He had so many wives to advise him." Teacher (a strong-minded female) : " Well, that is not the answer in the book, but you may go to the head." MRS. NEWED : "I've brought three of these eggeback to change them." Grocer: "They are strictly fresh, ma'am." Mrs. Newed : "No doubt; but the shells are brown, while my new egg cups are blue." HENRY ERSKINE, succeeding Pandas as Lord- Advocate, that good-humoured politician offered to lend him his embroidered official gown, as he would not want it long. "No," said he in the same spirit. "I will not assum• the abandoned habits of my

predecessors." ENGLISIIMAII—" Pardon me, sir, but where do you come from?" Paddy—" From County Cork." Englishman—" Then that accounts for your brogue." Paddy—" May I ax where you come from?" Englishman—" From Worcester, sir " proudly. Paddy—" Then that accounts for your satice." " WHAT have you decided to give Tom for his birthday ?" Mrs. Tom: "A nice collar and cuff box. It will be so convenient to keep my buttons, thread, and scissors in." MAN shows his teeth and growls; but woman shows her teeth and smiles, with far better chance of attaining her object. PRISON-WARDEN (t 0 condemned criminal MI morning of execution)—" I am to ask you if there is any little thing you would fancy for your breakfast." Criminal—" Thanks. I would like a couple of peaches.' Prison-warden—" Peaches. I Why, we are in March." Criminal—never mind. I can wait," A GOOD EGGS-AMPLE. —School Board Teacher: "Can any one tell me what an average is ? " Small Boy : "it's a thing a hen lays eggs on." Teacher: " Nonsense ? What are you talking about?" Small Boy • "I saw it in a book." Teacher (con- temptuously) ; "Show it me, then." Small boy produces a book and points to a sentence running. "A hen lays on an average four eggs a week." ARGUMENTUM At) FEMINAM.—OId Brute: "There is but one way to get the best of a woman in an argument." Young Brute: "What is that?" Old Brute : "State your side, and then laugh so loud that she can't make herself heard." A BLUNDER ALL ROUND —Wife (looking over bill) : "Do you remember my dear, how many trout you caught when tisaing last Saturday ?." Husband : "There were just twelve of 'em—all beauties ! Why ?" Wife: "The fishmonger has made a mistake; he only charges for half-a-dozen." TIIE AMERICAN CLIMATE. —Visitor : "What sort of weather did you have here this time last year?" Native. "Wall, really now, I don't just remember whether it was a drought or a flood.' WANTED ITALY THROWN IN.—Madame Parve- noo : "I want a first-class ticket to Rome." Agent (repres nting the Tourists' International Company): "Yes, ma'am." Madame Parvenoo : "And I want it to include an excursion to Italy, do you understand ?" ABLE TO WALK. —A visitor in Dublin was asked if he wanted a car by the car-driver. "No," said he, "I am able to walk." "May yer honour long be able, but seldom willing !" was the re- joinder. DIDN'T WANT TO REMAIN SINGLE. —At a party, the other evening, a Miss Joy was present, and in the course of the evening some one used the quota- tion, "A thing of beauty is a joy for ever,' when she exclaimed," Oh, I'm glad I'm not a beauty, for I shouldn't like to be a Joy for ever." • JUVENILE Wisnom.—Schoolmaster : "What are the teeth we get first called ?" Boy: "Milk teeth." Schoolmaster: "And those we get last ?" Boy : "False teeth." WHY HE LEFT. —Frangois (the new cook) : "I was very sorry to leave my place, but then, you see, my master was an amateur photographer." "Who, what difference did that make ?" "A great deal. He used to take a photograph of each joint before it left the dining-room?' Miss DE PRETTY: "I don't see how you whistle through your fingers that way. I could never do it in the world." Mr. Goodheart (wishing to compliment her delicate little hand) : "No, Miss de Pretty. If you should try it, your hand would .slip into your mouth." "You will, of course, immediately join in the mess, Mr. De Jones." said Adjutant Brown to the new ensign on the day of his arrival. "You are very kind, sir," stammered De Jones, "but the last promise which I made to my father was to avoid getting into any mess whatever." CAUGHT AT LAST. —Old Mrs. Townbred, visiting a cricket match for the first time, asked her niece,

who accompanied her, "why that man behind the wicket stopp €1 the balls that the other man wanted to hit." Soon after the wicket-keeper ca+,gltl, the batsman out, and some of the players shLited out, " Caught !" " !I am glad they've caught him at last," said the old lady, thinking it was the wicket-keeper they had caught), "the sneak! That makes the ninth time I've seen him stop the ball !" "OF COURSE SHE CAN.'—At a country fate a conjurer was performing the old trick of producing eggs from a pocket-handkerchief, when he remarked to a boy in front—" I say, my boy, yonr mother can't get eggs without hens, can she?" "Of course she can," was the reply. "Why, how 'is that?" asked the conjurer. "She keeps ducks," replied the boy. A MERCIFUL Junos:. "But, your honour;" pleaded the prisoner, " the physician's evidence is to the effect that I cannot live to serve a sentence of five years " "Inasmuch as the jury has recorn. mended you to the mercy of the court," responded his lordship, " and in view of the precarious condition of your health, therefore let it be known that I hereby reverse the sentence of five years, and make it one for life." BOTH BOYS.—Teacher : "Now, Willie, suppose you were to hand a playmate your last apple to take a portion, wouldn't you tell him to take the larger piece?" Willie: "No mom " "You wouldn't? Why ? " "Cos t'wouldn't be neces- sar v." UN DERGOING AN OPERATION. —A Yorkshire vicar • received the following notice regarding a marriage from a parishioner: "This is to give you notis that I and Miss Jemima Arabella Brearley is cumin' to your church on Saturday afternoon flex, to undergo the operation of matrimony at your hands. Please be prompt, as the cab is hired by the hour." rue " ooeiation " was performed in due course.

The winning of the Queen's Prize by a Canadian has aroused such public gratification in that colony that Lord Aberdeen, the Governor-General, has sent a special telegram of congratulation to the winner. He is, indeed, a native of the North of England. Mr. Hayhurst, who is twenty-seven years of age, was born at Kendal, in Westmorland, and emigrated to Canada no longer ago than 1892; he resides at the town of Hamilton, in Ontario, is a pattern- maker by trade, and is a private in the 13th Battal- ion of Canadian Rifle Volunteers. From 1886 to the date of his emigration he attended the Wimbledon and Bisley meetings, and in 1889 won the Prince of Wales' Prize.

There is nothing new under the sun. In some constituencies there has been talk of resort to an astute device whereby miners and others have been seduced from their political allegiance by the effort of book-makers, who by laying odds against the success of the man they wanted to get in have ensured votes for him. In the old days the same trick was resorted to, though in a form less veiled. Then the formula was, "I'll lay you five guineas and stake the money in yoar own hand that you do not vote for Mr. Fox." A vete for Mr. Fox followed as a natural consequence.

The changes which have taken place in the per- II sonel of the House of Commons, will not have the I result of strengthening it either in the matter of ability or character. The Liberal reverses have had I the effect ot driving for a time out of Parliamen- tary life a whole host of men enjoying some form of distinction for great intellectual ability, long Parliamentary experience, expert information on special subjects, on for mere personal eccentricity. To put the men of front rank aside altogether, the House will certainly miss such familiar figures as those of Mr. Howell, Mr. Cremer, and Mr. Rowlands among the old Labour party—all of them men who seemed to gave acquired a sort of vested interest. in their heats. For varied reasons Mr. Russell, Mr Robert Spencer, Mr. Caine, Mr. Naoroji,Sir E. Reed, Mr. S. Storey, Sir Charles Cameron, Mr. Hopwood —even Mr. Conybeare, Mr. A. C. Morton, and Mr. Eeir Hardie—will make their absence felt. They were all House of Commons " chsracters"—some by their personal weight, others by their identifica- tion with particular causes, and others, it must be confessed, only by their peculiarities ; and the House will not be the same without them.

On the other hand, it seems to be generally agreed that the men who have stepped into the shoes of the defeated Liberals are for the most part gentle- men of a very ordinary type, who will no doubt vote straight and do their duty according to their lights, but whose election does not, as Lord Rose- bery said a short time ago, "threaten an immedi- ate conflagration of the Thames!' Of course there may be some budding geniuses among them, but usually when a new member possesses any striking oratorical or ether gifts rumour to some extent heralds his approach. There was plenty of talk after the last general election as to the young men of the Liberal party. The old Unionist members who have found their way back to Parliament are certainly, as a rule, men of the commonplace type. At present the most remarkable figure added to the House of Commons by the electors is that of Mr. H. M. Stanley, but there is probably little that now remains to be discovered in regard to his special talent. Some interest is felt in regard to the elec- tion of the Marquis of Lorne, but this is purely, of course, because it is a very unusual thing for tte House to count among its members so cluse a con- nection of Royalty. However, it is just as well for the Government, no doubt, that they should not at the present time have too many able and ambitious young men added to their followers, seeing that so many are already suffering the pangs of disappoint- ment, The quarrel among the victors over the spoils has begun early. A very pretty dispute is in full swing and it is around the Speaker's chair, of all Parlia- mentary places, that the saviours of our Constitu- tion are quarrelling. They are wrangling and fighting with a vehemence which renders it certain that the chair itself must necessarily be besmirched and its trimmings torn. There are two things which by common consent have hitherto been regarded as outside the range of party football. The one is the Queen's name, the other the Speakership. Certain of our new constitutionalists seem to care little ' for the latter. Happily there are some clear-headed men among them who see the dangers surrounding I a dragging of the Speakership into the mud and strife of the electoral arena, and they are luckily raising a warning voice. Liberals meantime are looking on with amusement at these demonstrations of Conservative capacity for sacrilegious acts,inter- ested only to observe which section will prove the stronger in this game of "pull devil, pull baker." If the Conservatives choose to break down honour- able tradition it is not the Liberals who in the long run will be the losers.

The Shahzada cannot but be aware that we can- not have him here much longer, and now he has been informed that his Continental trip must be undertaken at his own expense. This visitor, who has so long overstayed his welcome, was to have departed for the Continent on Wednesday next. He now puts off his departure to an indefinite date. No one knows why, for he sleeps half the day, and the other half he is smoking and lazily driving about empty London. Mr. Stewart Bayley, the political secretary to the India Office, has n.,w ceased to have much to do with himas he has been appointed a member of the Indian Council, and the new poli- tical secretary, direct from India, Mr. Lee Warner, has not yet taken up the post.

Of Sir George Lewis, the famous lawyer, it has been said that he knows enough to hang half-a- dozen of the biggest men in the City. No man, however, will ever discover the secrets of which he is master, for Sir George, for many years,has ceased to keep an official diary, and when he dies the con- fidences of London society will die with him. The confidential nature of his calling made Sir George Lewis determine, some twenty years ago, never to chronicle the revelations made to his private ear, although all lawyers are expected to keep a record of this kind. He has been told from the bench, however, that under his peculiar circumstances no judge would ever blame him for his discretion. Never was a novel written or a play produced con- taining A =ll incidents and situations as are now awl for ever locked in the bosom of the confidential [friend of society's sinners.

A story is going about that Mr.Pritchard Morgan, Mr. David Thomas's colleague in the representation of Merthyr, proposes to retire in order that his sent may, subject to the approval of the electors, be placed at the disposal of Mr. John Morley. This is a constituency which is almost unrivalled in the wild fluctuations observable between this year and 1892. In the last-namel year the Liberal majority was 9,462; last week Mr. Pritchard Morgan beat his Conservative antagonist by a mere trifle of 2,029. There is an evident disposition on the .part of both the Prime Minister and the Secretary for War, to say nothing of anybody else, to reconsider the position of the Duke of Cambridge. Cernrounica- tions on the subject have, I am authoritatively in- formed, recently passed between the Duke and the War Office, and it is said that.the Queen herself has been brought into the discussion. Indeed in official circles it is regarded .118 practically certain either that some extension of office will be given to the Duke or that some extra service recognition will be granted to him.

News reaches me from an authoritative channel , in St. Petersburg that the !Maslen ant Greek Governments have just signed a convention which is calculated to have an important bearing upon the Caucasian oil trade. The Russian Governm.nt have for a long time been bent upon the creation of a monopoly in this particular trade to the exclusion alike of the Nobels and Rothschilds; and the con- vention which has just been signed, and which is to be in operation for ten years, may be taken as the first step towards the realisation of the plans to be carried out by the Czar's Government. In this connection it is further worthy of note that the llus,ians have also made the necessary surveys and actually given orders in England and France for material for the construction of some fifteen hun- dred miles of new railways.

By no means the least painful of the many tra- gedies which have attended the Liberator Societies is the death of Mr. Co'dwells, till recently M.P. for North Lambeth, and one of the defendants in the prosecution instituted against certain directors of the Liberator Society. Mr. Coldwells had risen from humble beginnings to considerable prosperity, when in an evil moment for himself he got en- tangled in the meshes of Balfourian finance. Hav- ing paid dearly for his indiscretion by the loss of his fortune, he has now further expiated them with his life.

A Roman shoo or sandal-maker was assisted in his business by twenty different deities. The popularity of precious stones now is : The pearl first, ruby second, and the diamond third. Iron has for ages been a favourite medicine. Nearly a hundred different preparations of iron are now known to the chemists.

The longest game of chess on record required between five and six years to play it. One player was in Eng- land and .one in Australia, and the game was played by post. A clear transparent cement, suitable for delicate articles, can be made by mixing rice flour with cold water and boiling it slowly. The facts of heredity show that as a rule the male takes the peculiarities of the father and the female those of the mother. The Greeks consume annually to each inhabitant five pounds of sugar and one pound of coffee. They make up the deficiency in wine, drinking eighteen gallons each In the twelve months.

Should anything get into the eye, one drop of castor oil should be dropped into the corner of it ; but if the intruding substance be mortar or lime bathe the eye with a weak solution of vinegar and water. Chimneys smoke because the carbon of the coal is dis- integrated and drawn off by the heat instead of beina consumed in the fire. A furnace properly tended would not smoke, as all the fuel would be consumed. A French physician says that biting the nail is a mark of incipient nervous degeneration. He believes it to be hereditary. From statistics gathered by him among school children, it is shown that almost one- third are nail biters, and that the habit is raore notice- able among girls than boys. Under the Merovingian dynasty in France the female costume consisted of a crimson gown with grayish-yellow bodice, gold broidered belt, blue cloak, and white veil fastened on the forehead with a gold band. The origin of the oft-quoted saying that the streets of London are paved with gold is somewhat curious. It seems that the granite cubes used for paving were called by contractors "half-sovereigns," and that in mediaeval times they were known "as sovereigns"; hence the saying. The accuracy of "finger prints" as a test of per- sonal identity is well shown by some recent photographs by Mr. Francis Galton. In a case of twins,their photo- graphs and measurements were closely alike, but the minutiae of their finger prints were quite different: An enlarged photograph of the print of the hand of a child eighty-six days old shows the development of the dis- tinctive little ridges on the skin even at that early age. A statistical work about the world's millionaires has just been published. While there are richer individuals in America, it says, most millionaires are to be found in Great Britain. But the figures must be taken as guess work, more or less. This is bow people possessing £1,000,000. or more, are divided among the nations : Great Britain, 200 ; United States, 100; Germany and Austria, 100; France, 75 ; Russia, 50 ; ludia, 50 ; all other countries, 125. If varnish is defaced and shows white marks, take equal parts of linseed oil and turpeutine,and shake them well together in a bottle ; apply a small quantity with a soft piece of cotton until the original is restored. Wipe the mixture off entirely, and polish with soft rag. Porcelain and earthenware are made from clay,which, while moistened with water so as to be of doughlike consistency, is shaped and then baked or partially vitri- fied by firing in a furnace. On removal from the fur- nace it may be coated with a fusible glaze and re-fired,so as to fuse the glaze. This completes the process,though, if it has to be decorated by painting, a third firing is necessary to fix the colour. An ocean liner like the New York puts to sea with about nine thousand napkins, ten thousand towels, six thousand or seven thousand sheets, eight thousand pil- low slips, andabout one thousand tablecloths. Most of these find their way to the soiled linen locker in the course of the voyage. When the vessel arrives in port they are carried off to a laundry operated by the com- pany, and made ready for the return trip.

Prize Babies. The child is the father of the man, and how interest- ing it would be to trace the subsequent history of prize babies and to ascertain if they furnish more distin- guished men and women to the world than those who did not start so well in life. Mrs. Robert Crawshaw re- dentiy held at her house an aristocratic baby show, which was very largely attended. The first prize for weight and general excellence for babies under one year of age was awarded to Dermot Browne, son of Lord and Lady Castlerosse, who, though but eleven months old weighed 32ilbs. The prize for weight and general ex- cellence of development for babies over one year of age was awarded to Angela Mildred Baring, daughter of the late Lord and Lady kshburton. who was 18 months old, weighed 281bs.,and had 14 teeth. Information as to the feeding of these children would have been interesting.

Poisoned by Coffee. Dr. Gilles de,la Tourette points out the possibility of poisoning by the inordinate consumption of coffee. Chronic coffee poisoning is almost always mistaken for the troubles engendered by the abuse of alcohol. In both cases the stomach and the nervous system bear the brunt of the attack. In effect, caffeic and alcoholic in- flammation of the stomach are nearly identical as to their symptoms—morning vomiting of glairy mucus, pain in the pit of the stomach, thickly-coated tongue, and loss of appetite. The disgust excited by even the idea of solid food is such that the sufferer eats nothing else but bread soaked in his poison—coffee. There supPr- vene then nausea, vomiting, and painful acid eructa- tions, and the sufferer finally becomes a victim to caffein cachrxia, or impoverishment of the blood. The circula- tory system becomes, in its turn, • ttacked, the pulse being slowed to a marked extent. Insomnia is common, and if sleep persist it is disturbed by the dreams of a terrifying or'' professional "nature, recalling the ner- vous disturbance met with in alcoholism. The drunk- ard's trembling ensues and cramps, often very painful, of the thigh and calf muscles are frequently noted. The symptoms are not persistent, the suppression of coffee sufficing to:bring about their prompt disappearancs The abuse of coffee by children has in several instances de- termined an arrest of development. It is not often that children make an immoderate use of coffee in England, but the same cannot certainly be said of tea, the alka- loid of which is identical with that of coffee. English parents would do well to restrict the supply of tea to children. Neglect of this rule may be responsible for many digestive and nervous troubles,the origin of which Is vainly sought for by the puzzled family medical at- tendant.

div.head: LADIES' LETTER.
div.p: LADIES' LETTER.

MY DEAREST NELLIE, One sees new blouses every day, and all of .them are pretty, especially those which are known as " washing " ones. A kind of holland coloured grass cloth is being very much worn; especially at seaside places in the neighbourhood of garrison towns, which points 'to the fact that the first ecru or buff grass cloth was brought over by officers' wives from India. For instance, there is a butter- coloured muslin blouse, with tight turndown collar and cuffs, and a centre pleat of-the same bordered with tine mauve cambric pleating edged with butter-coloured lace, very narrow indeed. This pleating is also made in pink and blue, but looks very much nicer and is more worn in mauve. I saw another dainty, girlish blouse of satin, which was veiled in net of the same tint, and trimmed in front with satin ribbons coming from under-arm seam and tied in a bow with a buckle of brilliants on the bust. The satin was .close-fitting, and the net gathered on very full, with a rather wide head- ing, which makes a pretty finish round the ifeck. Here is another, in white satin, which looks awfully nice for blouses. The one I refer to is striped with mauve, and is brocaded with pink flowers. It is trimmed with cream lace. A broad-brimmed hat turned up at one side may be woin with this blouse. It would .loOkApcy well in the new "sun-kissed" straw, with black wings and pink flowers, the cream lace being added as a trimming.

For home wear on summer evenings, or to slip on for afternoon tea, the semi-fitting tea jacket I saw last week is a delightful garment. Lining may be dispensed with, excepting just for the sleeves, where the pouff becomes loose and shape- less, unless mounted on a lining. There is only one side piece, and the fronts have no darts, but the fulness is collected in pleats, which are fixed by three rows of stitching in the waistline, and a velvet band passes over these. The centre plastron is simply the full front of the jacket, on which the narrow insertion is fixed, and the revers separate this from the remainder. The revers must be made quite stiff and firm with a double fold of muslin, and the full frills of lace are sewn on the inside. At the back there is a deep square tab or collar, starting from the revers, and also finished with lace. The basque is cut quite short at the back, and runs off to a point in front, and is also edged with lace. Another very lovely tea-gown is com- posed of mousseline de soir with stripes from shoulder to hem of lace.

As regards materials, the cool, fresh-looking muslins are equally popular with the equally dainty grass batistes and glace silks, and although some positively astounding combinations of colour are to be seen, such as cornflower-blue, bright pink, green, and shot hydrangea, all displayed on the gown and hat of one person, these are not worn by really well-dressed women. In fact the chief characteristic of really stylish toilettes is the per- fection of daintiness both in colour and make. Blue, as I have told you before, is emphatically the favourite colour this year, but lilac, pale pink, green, cream, and pure white are all more or less worn, and vary the predominant tint very pleasantly. Details, such as veils, neck ribbons, and gloves, are very carefully selected. Very fine veils of white or cream Brussels net, with lace border, are the most fashionable, and these are generally worn over the hat brims, instead of being put on first, as they were last year. Fine white tulle veils are also very becoming, but they are rather expensive, as the fabric crushes so easily. I forgot to mention a hat I saw a day or two ago. It was made of shot blue fancy straw, and had a straw ruche round the edge. The trimming

was shot blue and green ribbon, huge blue flowers with green centres, and purplish-tinted rose foliage. It was a lovely creation. Turning to capes, one of the newest mantles or capes is made of graduated gores of shot and black silk put in alternately from the neck, and the seams covered with very narrow ecru insertion. Down the centre of each gore is a series of eyelet holes worked in ecru silk, and at the bottom of each is a pointed motif of ecru passementerie laid on separately—so that the silk shows through for about half its length. The lower part of these pieces of passementerie is in a bold and handsome design, and falls about two inches below the cape. The ruffle round the neck is of ecru lazte edged chiffon. Your loving

div.head: What Women did in the Elections.
div.p: What Women did in the Elections.

The editor of the " Gentlewoman " has addressed an inquiry to every elected member of Parliament asking to what extent he attributes his success to the work of women at the election, in what ways they specially helped him, and if to a greater extent than at any pre- vious election. In response to this, in the present num- ber of the paper, Liberal and Conservative members alike bear witness to the splendid work done for them by women. Mr. Ritchie says :—" I attribute the mea- sure of my success at Croydon in a large degree to the splendid help of ladies, both in canyasung and getting voters to go to the poll. I have never seen anything like it before." Sir J. T. Wodehouse says: "I had the honour of winning at Huddersfield for the Liberal cause cal:at up to now has been the most splendid victory on our side, and I have, in response to your request, much plemure in testifying to the arduous and valuable work done by women workers. I cannot speak too warmly of their great help." Sir Frank Lockwood says :—" In canvassing in particular, Mr. Pease and I obtained great assistance from the work of women. To my mind, the greater interest women take in electoral matters the better it is for the constituency in which they work, whether they be Liberals or Tories." General Golds- worthy says that his address and polling cards, with en- closure, were entirely prepared for posting to 12,500 voters by the voluntary work of ladies. More women are evidently interested in politics than before, but very much has been done by ladies in the previous elections, and much praise is due to them.

div.head: EDISON INTENDS AIDING CYCLISTS.
div.p: EDISON INTENDS AIDING CYCLISTS.

An American correspondent informs us that Mr. Edison has been experimenting with an attachment to a bicycle for his own personal use and for special condi- tions. His house in Llewellyn Park,Orange,is about one- sixth of a mile from his laboratory and eighty feet higher up on the mountain side. So in order to save himself a heavy pull when he went home in the middle of the day be designed a heavy spring, just large enough for the purpose, which was to be wound up by power from the laboratory engine and attached to the bicycle before he started up the hill. He wanted this spring to supply most of the energy for the ascent. Of course, there is nothing electrical about it at all. It was a purely methsnical construction. This little contrivance caused Mr. Edison to wonder why springs are not made use of in bicycles or tricycles as accumulators of energy. It would be comparatively easy to adapt them for the purp )se. The device could be so arranged that when riding down hill, or even on a level, the rider could at will throw the spring into gear and by degrees wind it up to its limit. Then when A. hill was to he climbed, or the rider wished to stop working for a short distance on the level, he could turn on the power and let the spring give back some of the energy stored up in it. It could be arranged so that the spring cou'd be would up gradu- ally, so as not to make pedalling much heavier when on a level, and should, Mr. Edison thinks, be of sufficient power to carry a rider I,oooft. or so on a good road with no up grade without his doing any work.

CHAPTER Vt, THE SHIP. —DANGER A. The East India Company's- goon ship, 77te Golden Fleece, with a valuable cargo, both of mer- chandise and of treasure, sailed from Bristol near the middle of September. She was commanded by Warren Harlow, an experienced officer and thorough sailor, and was manned by an able and efficient crew. As other ships belonging to the company were upon the eve of departing from London, but few passengers had been registered for the Golden Fleece, most of those who had occa- sion, either for business or for pleasure, to make the voyage, preferring to take passage from the metropolis. Still our good Bristol ship carried passengers of note. First was General Sir Jasper Wallace, a brave and loyal knight of Devonshire, who had seen much service, and who was now on his way to India partly in hopes to recruit his shattered health, and partly on business of a private nature; for Sir Jasper had served under Clive in his younger days, and now held a material interest of no mean acccount in the company's domain of Bengal. He had reached the age of three score; but it was hard service rather than years which had stricken him. The ordinary duties of camp and field could never have shattered a frame like his, but several severe wounds, reaching towards vital points, had let out strength which he might never regain. His form was still erect, his mien dignified, and his bearing gentle and courteous. Though not on active duty, he still retained his commission and wore the military garb. Accompanying Sir Jasper was his niece, Mary Wallace, an orphan, and daughter of Sir Jasper's only sister, whom he had adopted as his own, and whom he loved with paternal pride and fondness. And well might the old soldier love that gentle maiden, for surely one more loving or lovable never fell to the care of a doting guardian. She was in her twentieth year, the very picture of health and vivacity; of that form and stature which best befits true female comeliness—neither slight nor stout, but just verging enough upon embonpoint to give substance and reality to her charms. Her skin was as pure as the purest marble of Faros, when, fresh from the chisel of the sculptor, it glows in the warm sunlight; her well-rounded cheeks bore a flush like that which blooms in the dewy depths of the blush-rose; her features were delicately harmonious, with those provoking dimples which gather up laughter and reflect in it smiles and sunshine; her eyes were of a rich hazel, warm and brilliantly beautiful ; and her hair, soft and fine as flossy silk, and sweeping away from her pure white brow into wavy tresses was of that lustrous brown which darkens in the shade, but glows with a golden sheen in the strong light. The only other passenger who joined in the cabin mess was Lord James Fitzjanies, the son of a Border marquis, who had money to spend, and who was going forth to see the world. "And I think," replied Mary, looking up with a sweet smile, "that we women, who are forced to depend so much upon your sex for guidance and protection, ought to estimate men in the same Way." While Captain Harlow stood entranced by the magic sweetness of the face that smiled upon him, and before he could frame further speech, Lord James Fitzjames, in a suit of crimson vel- vet, and with a gold-mounted quizzing-glass fixed Into the orbit of the right eye, entered upon the scene. " Avr,—pawdon f Ton my soul, how delightful. Dear lady, does not the pwospect of a voyage upon the vasty deep fill you with anticipations of ecstasy?" The captain smiled, and turned away. Mary elso smiled; but the little cirdets that lingered about the delicate dimples bore an unmistakable touch of displeasure, not to say of contempt. "I think I shall enjoy the voyage, my lord," she ' said; "that is, if we are- blessed with pleasant weather." " Ah, fair lady, your yews; pwesence ought to insure us against unpwesent weather. If the Storm-Spiwit dares to come where such—" " My lord !" She touched him upon the arm just in season to I warn him from the track of rough men who were 1 leading some of the rigging on deck. This broke the thread of his rhapsody, and he subsided into 1 a more rational mood. Before night the ship was well down in the chops of the channel, and a heavy swell which rolled in from the sea imparted to her a motion which was far from agreeable in its consequences-to those who were not used to the cradling of the ocean. Lord James Fitzjames was the first to succumb. He staggered down from the poop, and grasped his way into the cabin, looking very pale and very miserable. Nearly a week elipsed before the monster of sea-sickness let go of its victims, and during that time the ship stood upon her course under a fair wind. Arthur Rainsford, who had had much experience In yachting, and who had been accounted one of the most acomplished officers of his squadron, and who moreover, found little comfort in idleness, rendered much assistance to Capt. Harlow and to his lieutenants. He very soon formed the acquaint- ance of Sir Jasper, and that old soldier liked hirr from the start. " Zounds !" said the general, one day, in versation with his niece, what a pity to was,llo lordship upon such a piece of stuff as that, vT„her, there are men like young Rainsford who rra • ,ht adorn it ! " Lord Fitzjames had just left the cabin. Whatever may have been Mary's opinic4 a upon the subject she knew that her guardian,,had but given expression to a passing thought, an ,d she did , not feel called upon to reply. "By the way," pursued Sir Jasper, afto”r a pause "speaking of this young man brings tax' my mind that I once knew another of the same creame. But they cannot have been related. This ril4tainsford is from Yorkshire; the other Rainsfordwas " I think, never so far North." Shortly afterwards the general and 'his niece went - on deck. The bloom had returned to Mar 13. Ys cheek and the buoyancy had come back to her sp ,frita and if

She may prove the bright star that shall light us to victory." The youth's handsome features glowed wittf sublime effulgence as he spoke, and it was plain w be seen that he, at least, felt the full mean - the magic inspiration. And, moreover, the thanked him with a look that sent a ni thrill of motive power to his soul, in a transforming the eve of mortal danger of the most blissful periods of his life.

div.head: ORANG-OUTANG REVENGE.
div.p: ORANG-OUTANG REVENGE.

Vecial correspondent at Boekit-Tangah, Malacca, Rends, under daks of May 10th,the details of a most re- makable adventure with orang-outangs which will open , the eyes of naturalists all the world over. is story re- veals many curious traits of these little-known creatures and shows us that we are under great misconceptions regarding some of their characteristics. The following, however, is the narrative : "Although my house in this mountainous district is but four hours from Penang over the carriage route through the forest, one may reach the sea in hell that time on horseback along the river front. The nei,4llhour- hood abounds in wild animals, yet, until six weeks ago, I was not aware of the fact that the orang-outato,s arc numerous in these parts. I made the acquaint •trio of , the man-of-the-woods at the time mentioned when re- turninvr, from the coast on horseback. My Malay ser- vant, Pamba, a noted tiger hunter, fearless to the bone, was in tr.v company. .

" We came upon the apes quite unexpeetedly, within Bight of my farm house. There were thirty or forty of them, a fact which is quite contrary te the convictions of some of the noble gentlemen who write books on zoology. Instantaneously the memory of this sentence from an old-time text-book, ' Orang-outangs do not live in suci-ty, except when a pair has a family in charge,' revived in my mind,but the spectacle 'before me was not favourable te a reminiscent mood.

" The loose-haired apes were in a great state of ex- citement. They seemed to discuss amatter of immense consequence to themselves and screamed and shrieked wildly, gesticulating at the same time after the manner of the low Italians. All appeared to be above sft. high; indeed, many must have reached 7ft. When I first caught sight of the troop of apes'the majority were on all-fours, but now that their savageness increased they swung the body awkwardly forward between the arms, supporting it by their bent knuckles. Suddenly the entire mob turned against the orang-outang that stood in their midst like a prisoner. They heat him, using, as far as I could see, their left hands principally. Then a grey haired man-of-the-wools ltt out a terrifying screech, which was probably a signal, for immediately after- wards himself and all his mates began to tear to pieces the comrade condemned to ,death. I heard his bones break, so near was I to the place of execution. The orang-outang cried piteously.his voiceresembling that of a woman in sore distress. The novel quartering pro- cess lasted for about thirty to thirty-five seconds. is the orang-outangs formed a circle around the mutilated body of their victim I heard a shot. Pemba had fired in the midst of them. All fled but one, an old ape who rolled on the ground with a broken arm. The Malay advanced upon him, whereupon the animal ran off

My ser.vant i3a nativerof these parts and is intim- ately acquainted with its animal world. Ele gave as his opinion that these orang-outangs had never seen a ,white man and did not know anything of firearms*; the shot had startled and frightened them._ .

When we recounted our adventure at home my wife almost swooned away with terror. As it happened, she had received a visit from a missionary's wife, stationed in the interior of the peninsula,that very day, who had filled her mind with various stories descriptive of the orang-outang's ferocious and revengeful nature. To Booth her, I promised to go out of the way of orang- outangs thereafter. Pamba was ordered never under any circumstances to hunt them. I also ordered my servants not to go out into the forest alone, and to al- ways carry firearms when leaving the stockade. For myself and family I did not fear. The whites in this neighbourhood all wear duck or linen suits, the bright- ness of which frightens away animals, even tigers. Be- sides, we keep to the house after dark.

"About a week ago Pamba appeared breathlees in the dining-room, just as we wero sitting down to our even- ing meal. 'They have come,' he cried. -Bee for your- self, master.' "I walked out on to the veranda, and following the Malay's direction, observed a large nnmber of orang- outangs assembled at the end of the carriage-way lead- ing to my house. In front of them stood a colossal grey- , haired ape, who undoubtedly acted the part of the I leader. He was screeching and chattering away at a 1 tremendous rate, pointing towards us •as he did so. Look at his arm,' said Pamba. 'That is where my shot struck him.'

" It was indeed the orang-outang we had encountered, to his sorrow, some time ago. The longer I observed him the more convinced I became of the fact. 'We ought to teach him a lesson; I said. ' Fetch my guns.' Pamba, trembling with bloodthirstinfss, after the manner of his race, went and returned with lightning rapidity, but before we could raise the rifles to our cheeks, the orang-outangs had vanished. The servant was rather proud of the fact. Man-of-the-woods is smart animal,' he said ; • knows when he has enough. Will not stand in front of a gun: "Next morning we found the body of a native child in our front yard. The little one had been strangled to death. The nail marks at her neck were long and sharp. The orang-outangs had entered upon their campaign of revenge. " This death in the circle of natives intrusted to our care struck my poor wife as an evil omen. Her condi- tion became worse, and her excitability at last so pro- nounced that I decided to take her to 'Penang at once and send her home by the next mail steamer. Last Saturday afternoon at 3 o'clock our carriage was brought UD to the door. Pemba toOk me by the arm and said:: 'lf the master be wise he will wait until to-morrow and not drive through the forests, which is full of fero- cious beasts.'

I laughed away his misgivings. 'My good fellow,' I said, ' whoever heard of an attaok of wild animals on Europeans in broad daylight? 3un3p in th rear and take care of little Charley ; you may take my p stols if you will. The mistress and myself will take the box seats.'

"Master knows better than poor Pamba,' said the Malay, but I warn master of danger.' " Travel was comparatively easy during the first hour or so though the road grew worse all th-, time, the further we progressed on the way to sea. The Malay's evil predictions, though I would not admit it, had cast a shadow over the hopeful frame of mind in which I in- dulged. Now the forest became thicker, the road more uneven than ever, thorns and stones interfered with the gait of the pony. We had to go at a very slow pace. From Pamba not a word. My servant was a broad. cheated, copper-brown fellow with a fiat, nose, pr.qtrud- ing cheek bones and the straight, coarse hair of his race. In his lap rested my two pistols, from his girdle hung the kris, a two-edged knife, sharp as a razor, which the natives handle with astonishing dexterity. "Just as we were entering upon the second half of our journey we heard sounds over our heads in the trees. It was like, ' Tsjik-tsjik-tsjik:' " Man-of-the-wood is here,' said Pamba, stoically. I looked up. More than a dozen orang-outangs were watching us with gloating big eyes from above. And, as we proceeded, we observed that each tree forward on the road was manned by a couple of tailless apes. They are sentinels, having mounted guard over us,' whispered the Malay • and half a minute later he added, They are forming themselves into an army.' " A small troop, but a horrible one ! When we had passed the first guard-house tree, its hairy occupants let themselves down to the ground and trotted after us with uncertain, wavering steps, .crying their monotonous ITsjik-tsjik,' and showing their terrible teeth. The further we proceeded the more numerous the procession grew. " Our pony seemed to be aware of the danger. Before I could raise the whip he had entered upon a fast trot, and now broke into a gallop. I had seen enough of orang-outangs to know that the stories descriptive of their alleged inability to move swiftly alone the ground was incorrect. The black monsters were well able to keep pace with us. " Further and further towards the seaboard sped our brave pony, but horrors upon horrors, the number of sentinels above us, the army behind us, increased every ,mir.ute. Now I counted six apes in each tree on the road. Some of the monsters tried to jump into our carriage from the lower branches, but happily did not -calculate with the movements of the horse and all fell upon the ground. Suddenly an old ape alighted upon the step of the cart. His tremendous jaws for a moment opened not a foot from my face, and a whiff of his pol- luted breath struck my nostrils. At that moment Pamba's right, armed with an iron jimmy, descended upon the orang-outang's head, who fell to the ground with a terrible howl.

My wife, who had been leaning heavily upon me for some time, now swooned away, and my two little ones began to cry for help and mercy. recognised the im- possibility of escape by flight. Our cart was swinging from one side of the way to the other, and might turn over at any moment.

"When the troop of apes was about 75 feet distant from •us I ordered Pamba to fire. 'They will run away after the ,first shot,' I said to myself, doubting the truth of my own statement. The Malay, as if hp had followed my thoughts, said Man-of-woods knows that we cannot escape ; that he got us ; this time he will not turn tail.'

"One of the apes fell as a result of two shots fired ; the others continued to run after us. I handed Pamba my revolver. He waited until they were about 20ft, away, then fired six times in quick succession. For a second, or so, the animals seemed taken by surprise; they had probably.anticipated but one shot. Seeing two of their comrades drop they hesitated, conferred among themselves in their own shrill-toned language, then trotted on. The pony was panting and struggling hard for breath, and the next house was at least four miles away. " • Master must go ahead ; Pamba will fight man-of- the-wood," said the Malay after awhile. .• My head was swimming. With a dying wife and two little ones insane with fright, I hardly knew what I was doing, but I called out ; Take courage, boy ;we will yet escape them.'

div.head: AMINER, SATURDAY, AUGUST 3 1895. SPEECH DAY AT WARRINGTON GRAMMA.R SCHOOL.
div.p: THE AMINER, SATURDAY, AUGUST 3 1895. SPEECH DAY AT WARRING- TON GRAMMA.R SCHOOL.

" A minute later Pamba ryie, placed little Charley into my lap, and with a voice full of emotion,whipered ' God is good to white man. The master will look after Dhoba and Pamba's children. Good-bye master.' (Dhoba lIRIS the Malay's wife). " With that the brave fellow jumped from the wag- gon,in his right hand the glittering kris. I saw him face the army of apes, dealing terrific blows with his knife. Then, as my waggon turned the corner, he disappeared among the hundreds of bowling, screeching beasts. . .

" We arrived in Penang without furtheraccident. On the next morning I started act with ten well-armed men to search for Pemba. The orang-outangs had vanished. Pamba's body, tarn in flits' or more pieces, we found in the roadway surrounded by eleven dead apes, each one as big as a man. The erang-outang with the broken arm was among them."

The annual speech day at the Warrington Grammar School was held on Tuesday, and there was a very large number of ladies and gentlemen present. The head- master (the Rev. E. J. The proceedings were opened by the singing of the Latin hymn," 0, gorges (manes undique." THE MEAVMASTER'S REPORT. The HEAD Masirsa said It.ia my privilege to welcome you here once again thia afternoon, The past year has been for us an eventful one,and full of much encourage- ment. The mono:.ony and humdrum work of school life have been broken by many pleasing records of success both in the arena of examinations, and sports. The whole school has been examined, as usual, under the Oxford Local Examination Delegacy. The two highest forms,—the sixth and fifth—also sat for the certificates of profisiency granted by the University. We were for- tunate in passing sixteen of our candidates and securing seven muck coveted distinctions in various subjects. Our other successes during the year include—S. Walton. head boy of the school, first division in the London Uni- versity Matriculation examination ; E. A. Davies, a place among the successful candidates in the open com- petitive examination for boys'clerkships in her Majesty's Civil Service,; C. H. Ferguson, of University College, Liverpool, (I)., first examination for the degree of M. 8., Vic'xiria University ; (2), medal for biology, R. D. Willcocks, also of University College, Liverpool, first examination for the degree of 11.13., Victoria University. F. H. Gornall, a Cheshire County Council major scholarship in Owens College, Manches- ter, for a student about to engage in chemistry. J. H. Wright, scholar of Gonville and Cetus College, Cam- bridge, has graduated B.A. in the second class of the mathematical tripos. F. J. Ogden has won a place among the successful candidates in the open competi- tive examinations for clerkships of the second division in Her Majesty's Civil Service, and has been appointed to a clerkship in the War Office. J. C. Dewhurst has passed the qualifying examination of the Royal Institute of British Architects. W. H. Payton has passed the in- termediate examination for the degree of bachelor of music, Victoria University. W. A. Stone 8.A., late ex- hibitioner of this school and scholar of St. John's College, Cambridge, has been appointed to a form mastership in Bristol Grammar School. Mr. Stone was ordained a deacon on Trinity Sunday last in Wells Cathedral, and was the candidate selected by the Bishop of the Diocese to read the Gospel. H. Gorse, 8.A., late Beamont Ex- hibitioner of this school,scholar of Queen's College,Cam- bridge, has been appointed to an assistant mastership in the King's School, Rochester. Dr. J. G. °omen, M.A., M. 8., late scholar of St. Catharine's College, Cambridge, has qualified for the degree of D.P.H. (Diploma of Public Health)., granted by his University. I have heard of another appointment this morning,but I am told I must not mention it. I should like to have done an. I have to record,with much regret,the death of one of our most promising "alumni." The late Richard Fennelly's short career was a brilliant one, and gave hopes of uncommon success. He left us en winning an entrance scholarship at Owens College, Manchester. During his course there he obtained successively three other scholarships, and finally was elected to an open classical exhibition at Corpus Christi College, Oxford. Illness prevented him from eoing up to Oxford, and he died at Algiers at the close of last year. "Requiescat in pace." I have much pleasure in recording the distinction bestowed upon our second master, the Rev. L. B. Radford, who has been elected to a Fellowship of St. John's College,Cambridge. I take this opportunity of publicly congratulating him upon the honour he has done both to his own name,and also to the school with which he is connected. (Applause.) And at the same time I do not forget to recognize the hard work of my other colleagues, who have so loyally supported me—nor of the boys who have so heartily responded to our efforts on their behalf. Our best thanks are due to the donors of the two new prizes which have been founded since last year, viz., to Mr. Charles White, who has offered a prize for the best piece of original English verse, and to Miss Massey, who offers another for the best natural history collection. We have also to thank Mr. Alfred Woods for the beautifully designed and artistic silver medal which he gives each year to the holder of the school swimming challenge belt. There have been several changes on our governing body during the past rear, and the Hon. John Powys, Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bart., Mr. R. Ireland Blackburn, and Mr. James Fair- dough have been elected to fill the vacancies which have occurred. Before calling on the Rev. E. C. E. Carleton, whom we thank for his presence among us this after- noon, to distribute the prizes, I will read an extract from the examiner's report. The report itself is too long to be read in teens°, and has little interest for the general public, but I wish to give you his concluding remarks bearing on the two new prizes and on the work and tone of the school:—" I was much pleased with the compe- titions drawn forth by the offer of special prizes for Eng- lish verse and natural history specimens. In the former two copies of distinct merit were produced, Kidd's verse, translation of an 'Ode of Horace,' really deserv- ing to be described as a poetical effusion of much grace and choice diction. The natural history specimens of Hattori, consisting of local wild flowers, reflect great credit upon his industry and power of tasteful display. In conclusion, it gives me much pleasure, in spite of in- evitable criticisms, to reiterate my former opinion, that in their school the people of Warrington have an inatitu- tion of which they have good reason to to proud. In the work done, the best traditions of our old Grammar Schools are still preserved. Modern requirements are not neglected, while the claims of general culture are not altogether subordinated to those which are merely utilitarian. The governors of the school and the parents of scholars may continue to repose in the school, under its present able administration, the confidence which its past history has justly inspired. I cannot conclude without expressing, and this as no mere matter of form, but as the real outcome of my experience during the ex- amination, my beat thanks to the head master and his staff for the excellent arrangements, the perfect order, and the willing assistance which enabled me to get through my work with so much ease, and without any hitch whatever.—(Signed) J. Wonsur CIINDEY, M.A., Magdalen College, Oxford." (Applause.) THE PRIZE LIST.

SPEECH BY THE REV. E. C. E. CARLETON.

The Rev. E. C. E. CARLETON said that he thought that the fact that he was then to discharge that very impor- tant duty of distribnting the prizes was due to the personal feeling of friendliness of the headmaster rather than any qualification he had himself for so important an office. That office they knew had been filled by men in the past Of the highest eminence and position. With- out, however, offering any apology, he wished,he would no doubt as iar as his hearers were concerned, have the Indulgence he wished extended to one who appeared for the first tfme in a new part and that without a rehearsal. (Laughter.) They had heard the very excellent report read by the head master, a report which, he was sure, must be the cause of very great satisfaction to him, and to his colleagues, and also the source of very great pleasure to those present. The school took a very high class amongst the grammar schools of the country, and continued to maintain that position as a matter of course. Of course they only had that position secured by steady and self-denying application to duty on the part of the head master and his colleagues, and those who knew Mr. Willcocks at all, knew very well that he was not a man who did things by halves, and no pains were ever spared by him to make that school what it ought to be to the town of Warrington. He wished they could all realise the great boon the Inhabitants of Warrington had in the Beteler Grammar School. It was no burden on the rates which could not be said for many things in Warrington —(hear, hear)—and it offered educational advantages which were not elsewhere provided in the immediate locality, and it was one avenue by which parents of slender means could not only have their children pre- pared for professions, but likewise prepared for the universities and might be to some extent maintained at the universities. Thus he thought that such advantages were not to be found elsewhere in the locality, and was just the advantages necessary to those aspiring young men, that there were in such towns as Warrington, who desired perhaps to improve their position in the world and to win the honour and respect of their fellow men. They had had the names of some of the old boys read out that afternoon, and those young men were main- taining the creditof their old school at the University in a way that reflected no small honour upon themselves. (Applause.) They had heard their names, and there were others, and that not a few,who had passed through the school in the past who were filling honourable pro- fessions and important situations in various parts of the country, who were indebted for their success in life to their education at the Warrington Grammer School. (Applause.) He thought no one could doubt the advant- age that those endowed institutions were to the com- munity at large. Endowments were a kind of public revenue derived without the aid of taxation for Christian charity. It was a kind of charity in which they all participated, and which all accepted without any feeling of humiliation. It was, indeed, the Christian spirit that made charity something that they could accept without dishonour. They took their portion with just as little scruple as they took pocket money from their parents— (laughter)—and we should be very sorry indeed for the community at large to be deprived of this delightful illustration of what they owed to their common Christian profession. Be thought it a great boon for a country like this to have any source of income that did not arise from taxation, especially in those hard times, and they ought to be more grateful than they were for the income which the country derived from these sources. Taking in all the great public schools, universities, and charit- able institutions, without bringing in bodies of a purely ecclesiastical character, the income of the country ran up into several millions a year. Descending from generalities to particulars they had cause to be grateful for the admirable provision made by that good man Sir Thomas Boteler in the endowment of the school. He did no know what the endowment was beyond what he had seen:in rather an old copy of Baine's " History of Lancashire ;" but he supposed it was some- thing like £9OO a year. Well, now, that was a very handsome gift. He supposed to get anything like that income in these days they would have to invest some- thing like £30,000, a very nice sum. Well, he did not suppose that if any gentleman was to make a present of £30,000 to the people of Warrineton they would hide away the gift by erecting a building in connection with it on School-brow.He could quite understand that in days gone by this site for the school was by no means unsuit- able. In fact, before the development of the trade of the town in this direction, he had little doubt that it was a very eligible site, close to kindred institutions, near to the Parish Church,and on the outskirts of the town. But ' Warrington, like the other manufacturing towns of Lan- cashire,: had changed as it had grown and developed; and the interests of this public institution, and the de- sire to preserve to the town intact the fruits of Sir Thomas Boteler's liberality that it might serve the pur- pose for which it was intended,ought to make the people of Warrington consider whether the time had not come for the school to be placed in a situation where it would at least be better seen,and in which it would not appear as now, that they took less pride in it than they did in the Library, the Museum, the Post Office, even the Con- servative Club. (Applause.) He would say to his young friends in congratulating them on their year's work and on the recognition that it had met with on this very in- teresting occasion, that they must not mistake or mis- understand their present success or over value it. School education, and even college education, was only, after all,the beginning of the work that lay before them in life. It was well to have a good start, but that was not every- thing. And here lay the consolation for the boys that don't get prizes, or who seemed to be behind in their school competitions. The race was long enough to give the boys a chance who had not got staying power, and the alternate prize was better than the immediate prize. " Everything comes to him thaC waits" was,he believed a saying of Lord Beaconsfield's, who was himself a re- marka'ele illustration of the maxim. And even should they not attain a very tangible reward now, after all there was no reward that this world could give that was equal to the consciousness of having done th-jr best to be deserving, and to win commendation which, if not bestowed now, would most assuredly be bestowed here- after. (Applause.)

div.head: LATE WARR-INGTON BANE MANAGER AT LIVERPOOL ASSIZES.
div.p: A LATE WARR-INGTON BANE MANAGER AT LIVERPOOL ASSIZES.

Atthe Liverpool Assizes, on Friday, Elizabeth Darlow, money lender, Southport, brought an action to recover money under a promissory note, against John Black- burn, formerly a bank manager at Warrington, and a shopkeeper in Liverpool and Southport. The defendant counter-claimed £6OO for trespass at his shop at South- port.—The plaintiff was represented by Mr. Horridge, and Dr. O'reely appeared for the defendant.—'ln stating the case Mr. Horridge said be thought from the facts the jury would be of opinion that it was a matter in which a money lender had caught a tartar. (Laughter.) Mr. Eli Darlow was the manager for his wife, who was a money lender, and the promissory note, which was dated the 26'h November, 1894—given by the defendant to the plaintiff—was for £B5, to be paid in '5O weekly instalments of 28. each, in consideration of which D +flow advanced the defendant £4O. In the beginning of 1894 the defendant held the responsible position of manager of the Manchester Union Bank at Warrington, at a aalary of £3OO a year. He had also a lock-up shop in School-lane, Liverpool, and carried on a business there as 'Foster and Co. About April in that year he also took a shop for fancy goods in the name of Foster and 'Co., at 39a. Neville-street, South- port. When asked for a -reference, he referred the people to Mr. Blackburn, of the -Union Bank, Warrington, and in that capacity he gave Foster and Co.a good reference. Being in want of money, in November, 1894, be entered into negotiations with Darlow, to whom he stated that he was in receipt of a salary of £3OO, that he had a house of furniture worth nso, that his stock was of the value of £3OO. and that h did not owe more than £BO. On a promissory note to repay £65, together with an , assignment of the tenancy and fixtures of the shop at Southport and an authority to sell the goods, Darlow advanced £4O. Atthe beginning of December defen- dant suddenly left the bank, and the first instalment, due on the 3rd December, on the note, was not paid: It was ascertained that defendant's house at Warrington was closed, and that the shop at Southport was shut up and the landlord in possession for two quarters rent Darlow found a customer for the articles in the shop for £3O, out of which the rent was paid, and the balance. about £l3, taken by Darlow. The tenancy and fixtures were sold for £BO, which was handed to Mr. Hatch, auc- tioneer, to hold for three months in case of further de- velopments. The valuation of the business by defendant was £BO, so that a very good sale was effected, and therefore the counter claim was ridiculous. The plain. tiff would have been satisfied with the position of affairs but that defendant had insisted on going on with his counter claim. The plaintiff was clearly entitled to re- ziover under the promissory note., whatever might be the effect of the documents in regard to the shop. Evidence in support of the case for the plaintiff was given by Mr. Darlow, and in cross-examination he said that he would have advanced the money without the authority to sell the shop, for which defendant asked him to find a customer at once. lithe goods had been sold by auction as defendant suggested, they would not , have realised £lO. lie denied that the sale of the stock was bogus, and stated that he did not want to bring an action against the defendant, as he was not worth a penny and owed money. Witness did not remember defendant saying that he got his salary monthly, and that the instalments would be paid monthly and not weekly. John Hatch, auctioneer, said that £6O for the tenancy and fixtures was a good sale. The articles in the shop, he thought, would not realise £lO by auction. Walter Thatcher, stated that when he left the shop in Neville-st. to defendant, the latter represented himself as Foster, and gave sea reference the bank manager at Warrington.—Other evidence having been given, Dr. O'Feely stated that this was a remarkable case, and many painful and unnecessary matters had been in- troduced. Defendent had fallen into the hands of Dar- low,who was not contented with holding the goods in the shop as security,but who secured a promissory note and the assignment of the business. The stock in the shop was worth over £250 : and if that was not its value when it was seen by plaintiff's witnesses, then there was some mystery about the matter. When the money was lent, defendant told Darlow that he was paid his salary monthly.and that the instalments would be met monthly. To this Darlow agreed. As a matter of fact, the in- stalments of the £65 were only two weeks unpaid. and interest WAR charred, he contended, at the rate of 200 per cent.-25 Bs. 4d. for two weeks. Plaintiff had had his pound of fiesh,and that was why he did not wish to come into court. The entry and seizure of the goods in the shop, he argued, under the document in the case, were illegal, and defendantclaimed compensation. John Blackburn said that for four years he managed the Warrington branch of the Union Bank of Man- chester. He was asked to resign because the directors were of opinion that he could not attend to the bank affairs and carry on a basiness of his own. He in- formed Darlow of the resignation of his bank situation. The stock in the shop just before the sale cost about £250, soda good profit was expected. Joseph M. Lyons, auctioneer, stated that he saw the stock in the shop at the time in question, and he was sure it would bring by auction about £lOO or £125. Other evidence of a similar character having been heard, his Lordship, id summing up, said that it was abominable business that of money lending at £2OO per I cent, to people who were certain to be sold up. Both ' parties in this case were thoroughly disentitled to sym- pathy and respect, and the jury would have to choose between two people,on neither of whom they could place implicit reliance. The jury found that there was no verbal agreement that the instalments should be paid monthly and not weekly, and that the value ot the stock in the shop was £7O. His Lordship said that meant that plaintiff would re- cover on her claim £7O 83. 41, and the defendant would recover on his counter claim .270, and that judgment wonld be entered for the lefendant for £37 163 81.,heing the difference between the amount due to plaintiff by the defendant and the value of the stock and business.

div.head: SHIP CANAL.
div.p: SHIP CANAL.
LANCASHIRE COTTON SPINNERS AND THE SHIP CANAL.

About 200 representatives of cotton spinning firms and others interested in the success of the undertaking had a trip on Saturday on the Manchester Ship Canal from Pomona Docks to Liverpool under the auspices of the Manchester Cotton Association, which has been formed to secure the direct importation of cotton to Manchester. It is calculated that direct importation will save i. per lb. on the cotton. The association was not formed in time to have much influence upon the importation of last season's crop, but great hopes are entertained that a substantial portion of the trade of the nest season, which commences shortly, will be securea. The trip on Saturday was intended as a move in that direction. The members of the association re- present 14,000,000 spindles out of 40,000,000, and many influential spinners were included in the party. Speeches were delivered by Mr. C. W.Macara (president of the association), Mr. J. K. Bythell (chairman of the Ship Canal Company), Mr. Rueben Spencer,and some of the Oldham spinners, to the effect that the trade must secure the benefit of the cheaper cost of transit now open. Mr. C. W. Micara, in his observations, said he was sure all present must be impressed with the fact that the Ship Canal was quite capable of fulfilling what it had been made for In passing down it they had seen vessels of the very largest class that were used for the transit of goods. Alreadv,directly and directly, the canal had been of great benefit to the trade of Lancashire. There had not only been the saving on the limited amount of traffic which had been secured, but there had been a far greater saving through the reduction of rail- way rates, the two amounts being sufficient to pay a very substantial rate of interest on the whole under- taking. There was a duty lying upon every man in Lancashire to stand by that great undertaking. Nearly £150,000 a year could be saved if the raw cotton came direct to Manchester, and another £150,000 if the manufactured goods were shipped by the canal. It was not necessary to put the brokers in Liverpool to the expense at first of opening offices in Manchester. They would be perfectly willing to buy cotton at Liverpool which was lying at Manchester, if those concerned would send them the cotton they required,and not that which had been rejected at Liverpool. (Hear, hear.)

DARESDURY PARISII NURSE. . -

I Miss M. A. Jepson, of Bolton--Te-sa,•Carnforth, commenced duty en Monday as nurse to the Vicar of Daresbury's Nurse Association in place of Miss Ashton, resigned. ALTERATIONS AT PARR'S BANKING COMPANY LIVERPOOL OFFICE.

Mr. W. C. Ashtlin retires at the end of this month after a long and Nmourable service. Mr. John Stewart, formerly of the Bank of Scotland, Aber- deen, has been appointed manager, Mr. William D. Hughes, formerly in charge of the securities department, has been appointed sub-manager. RETURN OF THE MILITIA. The 3rd and 4th King's Liverpool Regiment ar- rived in Warrington on Saturday about one o'clock, after having completed their annual training at Altcar. The men looked remarkably well, and werp much sunburnt. On reaching the Barracks the men were "paid off" and dismissed. No disturb- ances of any kind occurred.

STABLE FIRE AT. WARRINGTOM-:- - On Tuesday night a fire broke out at the stables of Mr. William Parkinson, hay and straw dealer, Cloth Hall-yard. It is said that some lads were playing near the building when they threw some matches underneath the door. The building was soon in flames, but two reels were quickly secured and the fire extinguished in good time by Superin- tendent Turner and his men. The damage is esti- mated at from ..E5 to £6. P S.A. AT THE Y.M.C.A,

On Sunday there was a full attendance of mem- bers in connection with the P.S.A., and a hearty, helpful meeting was presided over by Mr. George Bayley, Clarionet solos were rendered at intervals by Mr. Adcroft, and were well performed. Mr. W. Light gave an earnest and practical address, hold- ing the audience in rapt attention. Mr. Holford and Mr. Stewart also assisted in the meeting,which terminated promptly at four o'clock. Mr. F. Hick- man was the accompanist. DARESBUILY SUNDAY SCHOOL.TREAT.

On Tuesday the Church Sunday School scholars from Daresbury,Preston Brook Mission-room,lloore, and Hatton had their annual summer treat to Over- ton Hills, Frodsbam. The party, together with teachers and a few parents, numbered about 200, and a start was made in 'buses for the different schools soon after dinner, arriving at Frodsharri Church about two, A start was made for home at 0.30 p.m. and Daresbury was reached a little after eight, a most enjoyable outing having been spelt, the weather being most favourable. - FEAST OF THE PATRON SAINT AT STv, JAMES' CH uncir. _ _ _

Sunday, being the 8-11-claiOf the Octave, special services were held in the above church. The first service was a celebration of the Holy Communion at 8 a.m., the second the usual morning service at 10.40 o'clock, when the pulpit was occupied by the Rev. Canon Willis. In the afternoon a flower ser- vice was held, when there were many children [ present, and a large number of beautiful flowers I were given. At 6.30 there was a festal evensong with band accompaniment. The Rev. Canon Willis again occupied the pulpit, and delivered another interesting sermon. There were large congrega- tions, and a special collection was made at each service in aid of the church expenses. PADGATE CHURCH SCHOOL SERMONS.

On Sunday the annual sermons in connection with Christ Church Schools, Padgate, were preached morning and evening. The weather was fine, and large congregations attended each service. The preacher in the morning was the Rev. Canon Penrhyn, rector of Winwick ; whilst in the evening the pulpit was occupied by the Rev. J. Sanders, M.A., vicar of Gateacre. The services were intoned by the Rev. J. J. Langhato. Special hymns were sung, and at the morning service the choir ren- dered the anthem commencing" Praise the Lord, 0 my soul " (103rd Psaim), in a tasteful manner, Mr. William Fryer singing the tenor solo with good effect. The anthem in the evening was " I will sing of Thy power "(Sullivan), Mr. Fryer again taking the tenor solo. Mr. Frank Blackwell was at his usual place, the organ. Offertories were taken in aid of the day and Sunday schools,and amounted to more than .£l3. PROPOSED CHANGES IN GOODS CARRYING. At the monthly meeting of the Warrington Cham- ber of Commerce which was held at the Offices, Market-gate, on Monday afternoon, the Hon_ Secretary (Councillor A. Bennett) reported that he had submitted a series of questions to the Parlia- mentary candidates for the district in reference to the abolition of the preferential railway rates on foreign produce and manufactures, the furnishing of traders and agriculturists with the right of ap- peal against any railway rates or charges which they considered to be unreasonable, and the freeing of the canals from the control of the railway com- panies. Replies had been received from Messrs. Robert Pierpoint, l'ercival B. Scott, and James Moon, and the Hon. T. W. Legh, all of which were more or less favourable to the objects which the Chamber had in view.—Tbe Secretary informed the Chamber that Mr. Robert Pierpoint, 31. P., had ac- companied the recent deputation to the Earl of Rosebery with the object of promoting an improved system of inter-imperial postal and telegraphic routes, to which object the Earl of Rosebery had replied in a satisfactory manner.—The mem- bers of the Chamber also discussed the present position of the negotiations between the Corpora- tion and the Ship Canal Company. WATER POLO MATCH.—WARRINGTON V. LIVERPOOL

div.head: CRESCENT S.C.
div.p: CRESCENT S.C.

A match between Warrington and Liverpool Crescent was played in the Warrington baths on Tuesday evening, before 200 spectators. A great amount of enthusiasm existed amongst the specta- tors, who often gave expression to their admira- tion of the tactics of the home men during the game. Throughout the contest the Warringtonians were clearly the better team, their excellent passing completely mastering the visitors. In the first half the locals secured five goals, which they increased to ten in the second half. A few minutes before the finish of play,Warrington began to take matters rather easy, and allowed the Crescent to obtain two goals, the final score being Warrington S.C., ten goals ; Liverpool Crescent, two goals. Scotson, Locker, Furness, Creighton, and Beaman were amongst the scorers,and played a capital game. FATAL ACCIDENT AT PADGATE,

Mr. F. A. Jones, deputy coroner, held an inquest on Wednesday, at the Imperial Hotel, Bewsey-at., onthe body of William Mills,aged 68 years,residing at 2, George-at., Bewsey-at., who died on Monday from injuries received from falling from a cart on July 2nd.—Elizabeth Mills said that the deceased was her husband, and was a joiner on the London and North-Vi. estern Railway. She saw him leave home on July 2nd., to go to Padgate with a cart containing a pig. He was brought back about nine o'clock severely injured on the shoulder. He was attended to by Dr. Adams up to the date of his death on Monday. The doct,or said thet he thought the deceased had ruptured a blood vessel—Thomas Johnson, 29, Catherine-st., said he went with de- ceased to radgate in the cart. At about 7.30 about 20 yards from the Ring and Queen, Padgate, the deceased who was sober, was driving. Suddenly the trolly broke, and witness, dneased, and a man named Crank fell out. Deceased fell on to bia shoulder against the parapet. He complained of being badly hurt in the back. He was a very stout man.—William C. Crank also gay.' evidence in cor- roboration of the last witness. The jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death."
