had considerable effect. This circular appears to have the intention of appealing on behalf of the Wesleyan body to the electors to support the Con- servatives against Home Rule for Ireland, on the ground that the Methodists in Ireland would be persecuted and worse, if Home Rule were granted. No one finds fault with these gentlemen for having opinions of their own, but when they issue mani- festoes they should not make it appear that they represent the Wesleyan ministers,for they do noth- ing of the kind. It is an undoubted fact that nine- tenths of the Wesleyan ministers in this country are Liberals, but they do not meddle with politics so obtrusively as the political parsons so often do on the other side.

The voting at the election in Warrington shows one thing] very clearly, namely, that the Liberals of the town have not their share of representation on the Town Council. If they were represented on that body according to the voting, there would be something like 20 To ies to 16 Liberals. As there are only 10 Liberals to 26 Tories,the latter are decidedly more numerous than they should be. This state of things may, how ever, be rectified if the Liberals of the town show, the same unanimity and heartiness at the next municipal elections that they showed last week.

There are a few State pensioners in Lord Salis- bury's new Government, bat it contains more than a few company promoters and company directors. According to Mr. A. J. Wilson of the "Investors' Review," twenty-five of the Ministers are the hol- ders of sixty-two directorships and trusteeships, and yet re are told tLat it is " slightly cleaner in the matter of company dabbling" than Lord Salis- bury's last Ministry was. Mr. Wilson speaks of the Government as " this truculent Ministry of Lord Salisbury's, with its curious mixture of autocratic, bagman, beer-brewing, pawnbroking,company-pro- moting,guinea-pigging,and stock-jobbing elements.' Even then he says he does not take into account " the kennel superintendents, upper stable boys, and other ornamental lacquey members of the Government, as it does not much matter what they do with their names and time." There is certainly a good deal to be said for Mr. Wilson's contention that no Minister should during his tenure of office remain a member of any public company whatever and the members of Lord Rosebery's government set a good example in severing their connections as directors with the public companies.

div.head: CHARGE OF BI7RGL4&RY AT RUNCORN.
div.p: CHARGE OF BI7RGL4&RY AT RUNCORN.
A STRUGGLE IN THE STREETS.

At Runcorn Police Court on Wednesday morning George Harvey, 30 years of age, of Grosvener-street, Runcorn,was brought up on remand before Mr.J.Brand- rit (chairnaan) and Mr.S.Taylor, charged with burglari- ()ugly entering the dwelling-house of Emma Bagley, Brunswick-Bt., Runcorn, at 1.30 a.m., on the 27th July, and stealing one clock, eno ulster, three hats, one dress and mackintosh, value 25i. Bd., the property of Emma Bagley; and also with burglariously breaking and enter- ing the house of Thomas William Darwell,Speakman-st., between 9 p.m. on the 28th July and 1.30 a.m. on the 27th, and stealing one pair of women's boots, value 34. 6d.. the goods of Elizabeth Darwell. Mr. Burton, solicitor, Runcorn, represented the prisoner. Emma Bagley, wife of Richard Bagley, stated that she kept a milk shop at 2,Brunswick-st. On Friday night last they went to bed about half-past ten, and at that time all the windows and doors were securely fastened. She was awakened in the night time by Sergeant Lee coming upstairs, and in consequence of what he said, she went downstairs. The sergeant picked up some things he saw lying in the yard, viz., a cloak, cape, dress, three hats, and mackintosh produced. These articles were hung up behind the kitchen door when they retired to rest. The clock and knife produeed,also belonged to witness.—ln cross-examination by Superin- endent Atherton,witness admitted that there was a pane of glass broken in the back-kitchen window and that would enable anyone to get the knife from inside.— Jessie Reese stated that she was the daughter of the previous witness, and lived with her. The ulster and hat produced belonged to witness. On being awakened at twe o'clock on Saturday morning she went down- stairs and found a number of drawers open, and the contents thrown about the floor. She did not know the prisoner.—Sarah Ann Kelly, 10, Brunswick-st., deposed that she stayed at the house of Mrs. Bagley on the night in question. The hat and mackintosh produced were hers, and she left them behind the kitchen door.— Elizabeth Percival, 8, Alcock-st., identified the skirt and hat produced as her property. She had left them hang- ing up in Mrs. Bagley's kitchen. She slept at her house Ithat night. —Sergeant Lee stated that about 1.30 on the morning of the 27th July, he was on duty in Brunswick- street. He heard a noise in Massey's-Court, off Bruns- wick-street. On getting to the top of the entry leading to the court, he saw a man coming out of Bagley's back yard door. He was carrying a bundle in his hand. When he saw witness he backed into the yard. Witness went towards him and the prisoner rushed out and struck him, knocking him against the wall. He then ran in Brunswick-street and witness followed him. When reaching Brunswick school, the prisoner threw a boot at him. Prisoner again ran on, with witness in pursuit. On reaching the Anchor Inn, he pulled the clock from under his coat and said " If you come any further I will kill you." Prisoner raised the clock and tried to strike witness on the head with it, hut witness drew himself aside and the clock fell over his shoulder to the ground. Witness closed with prisoner, and a severe etruggletook place which lasted about half-an-hour. The prisoner tought very violently, kicking witness several times on the leg and body. He, at length, secured prisoner, and brought him to the Pollee Station. Witness then returned, and picked up the clock. On going to Bagley's yard door, where the prisoner had been standing, he found the articles produced. He noticed that the kitchen window was open, and on the sill there was a knife. Between the window frames it was possible to move the I catch of the window with the knife. The frame had been cut quite recently. The paraffin lamp was lighted in the kitchen, and the clothing from a chest of drawers was lying on the floor. He aroused the inmates and they identified the articles produced. On returning to the police station,he charged prisoner with the offence, and in reply he said, " Oh God do let me go home, if you keep me here you will ruin me for life." He was sober at the time.—ln answer to Mr. Burton, witness said he had not inquired as to the prisoner's character. ")91r. Burton, on behalf of the prisoner, said he would reserve the defence. With regard to the second charge, Elizabeth Darwell, Speakman-street, stated that at midnight on Friday, the 28,h July, she was lying on the sofa in the kitchen waiting for one of her sons to come in. The door of the hitched was closed but not locked. Whilst lying down she heard someone come in the back-kitcrhen. She thought it was her son and called out "James " twice, but on receiving no answer she got up and closed the back kitchen door which she found wide open,and heard someone going down the yard on their toes. She locked the door, and aeon afterwards someone knocked at the back-kitchen window. She was frightened and took the lamp upstairs, and did not come down again until day- light. The pair of boots produced were her property, and were placed under the table in the back kitchen be- fore she lay down. She had only taken the boots off about an hour previously, and did not miss them until Sergeant Lee came to her house earlythe same morning. Emma Bagley re-called, gave evidence as to Sergeant Lee finding one of the boots produced in her yard, and also to finding one boot herself in Brunswick-st.--Ser- geant Lee deposed that on Saturday morning last he charged the prisoner with stealing the boots, and he said "I know nothing about it."--The defence, with regard to this charge was also reserved. The prisoner was committed on both charges to the next County Aqsizes.—Mr. Burton said the Assizes would not be held until October, and he applied for bail. The prisoner had resided at Runcorn all his life and up to the Present, he bore an exceedingly good character. On the 4th July, the prisoner lost a Mlle child, and since that time there 'lad been a marked difference noticed in his behaviour and demeanour, and more especially during the last week or two. Certain evidence would be ad- duced that at the time of the offence;, the prisoner did not know what was taking Place. He was under the iufluence of drink and his mind was unhinged by the sufferinghe had endured.-4uperintenient Atherton said he must ask for substantial hail.—Pristmer was allowed bail, himself in a sum of £4O, and two sureties of £2O each.

div.head: WORICPEOPLE's TRIP_ TO SOUTHPORT.
div.p: WORICPEOPLE's TRIP_ TO SOUTHPORT.

On Saturday, the workpeople at Elighfield Tannery, with their wives and friends, numbering atout 140,were provided with a most enjoyable trip to Southport through the generosity of the directors of the company. ' The party left Runcorn at 10 o'clock and on arrival in Southport dispersed themselves in various directions. In the afternoen they all assembled at Churchtown Gardens where a good tea was provided for them. Home was safely reached about 10 o'clock, all being delighted with the outing. ACCIDENT TO AN OLD MAN. Early on Sunday morning, a man named Stephen Lowe, 60 years of age, and residing at 47, Surrey-streei., feel downstairs and sustained serious injuries. He appears to have missed his footing and fallen from top to bottom. His head struck the flags. He was examined by Dr. Robinson who found that he had sustained a dis- location of the upper portion of the spine. Through the efforts of Dr. Annett, assistant to Dr. Robinson, an order was obtained for his admission into the Royal Infirmary, Liverpool, whither he was conveyed on the St. John Ambulance carriage, on Sunday night. He was accom- panied by Mr. Bankes, one of the officers of the St. John , Ambulance Association. CHOIR SERMONS.

The Runcorn Psrish Church choir sermons were preached on Sunday, when the Rev. G. D. Wray, vicar ef Halton, preached in the morning, and the Rev. J. Holden, of Antrobus, in the evening. The musical por- tion of the services was a special feature. At the morn- ing service, the choir efficiently rendered Sullivan's anthem "Who is like unto Thee, 0 Lord?" and in the evening they sang Goss's anthem "Praise the Lord, 0 my soul." The quartette especially was well executed. Mr. James Littler was the conductor, and is to be con- gratulated upon the success of his efforts. Mr. Johnson occupied his accustomed place at the organ. The collec- tions realized £l4 Be. 9d., which is some £3 below those ' of 12 months ago. RUNCORN CO-OPERATIVE SOCIETY, LIMITED. The annual meeting of the members of this society will be held in the Public Hall, Runcorn, on Tuesday evening, particulars of which will be found in our ad- vertising columns. From the 66th half-yearly report. ending June 29th, it appears that the total sales amount to £44,122 10s. 60., being a decrease of £lBl 15s. 7-id. on the corresponding half-year. The amount disposable. after charging all expenses, including depreciation and interest on capital, deducting the cheques purchased, and reducing Ship Canal Shares £6O, is £6046 18s. Thd. A dividend of 2s. 9d. in the £ is recommended on £43,700 of check account books brought in,which would amount to £6,008 155.9 leaving a balance of £3B 35.70. to the reserve fund. The report is signed on behalf of the committee by William Rhodes, William Cropper, John Rogerson, and by William Upton, secretary. The annual excursion to Blackpool is to be held on Monday, Augu it 19th. LOCAL VOLUNTEERS AT DRILL. . .

The volunteers composing the 2nd Earl of Chester's Regiment, who to-day (Saturday) are to proceed to camp at Blackpool, had their annual battalion drill on Satur- I day afternoon. The members of the various companies at Chester, Frodsham and Hartford journeyed by special train to Runcorn and were met at the station by the Runcorn detachment. Headed by the band they pro- ceeded to a field near the Grange, which had been lent for the occasion by Mrs. Hazlehurst. The number on .parade was 18 officers, 45 sergeants, 55 band, pioneers, and signallers, and 340 rank and file. The officers present included Colonel Ashton, Major Hazieburst, Captain and Adjutant Turton, Hon. Major Dutton, Cap- tains Smith, Thompson, Harrison, atmon, and G. F. Ashton ; Lieutenants Brundrit, Evans, Bromley, Nichol- son, Rule, and Thornley. Ai ter the march past, which was satisfactorily performed, manual and firing exercises were engaged in under the command of Major Haztehurst. Colonel Ashton then put the men through various drill exercises, 'which were followed by the attack. At the close Colonel Ashton congratulated the various companies on turning out in such strong force, and complimented them upon the efficiency with which they had gone through the different movements. The men were afterwards provided with refreshments, and the officers were entertained by Mrs. lisziehurst, who was thanked for her kindness on the proposition of the chaplain, Rev. Dr. Preston. PROPOSED TREAT FOR POOR CHILDREN. A meeting of the Runcorn Aged Persons and Poor Children's Treat Committee was held at the Town Hall Runcorn, on Tuesday evening for the purpose of con- sidering the question of the poor children's treat. The chair was occupied by Mr. S. Taylor, J.P., C.C., and there were present the Revs.Dr.Gastaldi,J.Stafford,H.B. Firth, Messrs. E. Marshall, H. J. Grice, M. Sweetman, J. Wilson, T. C. Williams, Thomas Reynolds, John Smith J. Percival, Leach, and the three hon. secretaries,Messrs. J. D. Jones, T. Cooke, and W. Millington.—The Chair- man mentioned that there had been some question as to the advisability of holding a treat this year owing to the depressed condition of trade, which had been so keenly felt by tradesmen and townspeople generally. But for his part he thouAht it would be a very great pity to let it fall through, and he thought they should make an effort to carry the treat on as before.—Mr. Grice asked what funds were in hand, and in renly the chair- man said the total cost of the treat was £27, and the a- mount in hand was £lO 7s. 61.—Mr. Thomas Reynolds thought there were surely gentlemen in the town with hearts big enough and pockets big enough to raise the small matter of £l7.—Mr. Grice was of the same opinion, and thought they would easily be able to raise the required amount.—Dr. Gastaldi referred to the good, both morally and phy- sically the children derived from the treat. He thought there would be no difficulty in getting the money, but he was of the opinion that it would be in- advisable to call upon the tradesmen and shopkeepers of the town as they had suffered greatly by the trade de- pression. It was ultimately decided on the proposition of Mr. E. Marshall, seconded lw the Rev. Dr. Gastaldi, that the treat be again held this year. It was also de- cided that the children should be taken to Overton on the 21st August and provided with tea. A scrutiny com- mittee consisting of Messrs. Cooke, IC. Bowyer, Howard, Percival, Reynolds,John Smith and G. H. Kirkham were appointed to decide upon the children who were to par- ticipate in the treat. Each member of the committee was asked to submit names of children for the treat. The age was fixed at from 7 to 13.—A long conversation took place as to the best means of raising the money re- quired, and it was decided that members of the com- mittee should collect. A number of subscriptions were promised in the room. SUNDAY SCHOOL TREAT. _ _ . .

The scholars— 'attending Congregational School were provided with their annual treat on Wed- nesday, when they proceeded by train to Frodsham and then betook themselves to Overton hills where they en- joyed themselves immensely in various games. Tea was provided, and after romping about until dusk, they wended their way to the railway station, departing for Runcorn at 7.45. The Rev. J. S. Simpson accompanied the scholars.—Those attending the Primitive Methodist Sunday school, numbering about 250, also had their annual treat at Overton onWednesday. Amongst those present were the Rev. T. Braman, Messrs. J. Wilson, Hillidire, Fleet, Gittiens and Aston. The outing was greatly enjoyed. IMPORTANT PROPERTY SALE..

Messrs. WillTaVl—Wilson and Son, auctioneers, con- ducted a property sale at Wilson's Hotel, Runcorn, on Wednesday afternoon, in accordance with instructions from Wright's trustees, for the purpose of winding up an old trust. There was a large attendance, and a number of lots were disoosed of. For ground rents of property In Bold-st., Fisher-st., Stanley-st., and Irwell-lane, the prices at which they were sold was as follows :—For a yearly ground rent of £5 91., £145; £9 83. 3d., £252 103. ; £lO 17s. 61., £291; £lO 8;. 101, £285; £9 113. 6 /., £260; £6 155., £180; £2 83. Bd., £65; and £5 4i., £l4O. The dwelling-house occupied by Miss Warner at 40, Irwell-lane, with an annual ground rent of £1 164. Bd. was knocked down to Mr. Littler for £l3O. The Bridge- water trustees were the purchasers for £l,BOO, of a plot of land containing 4a. 2r. IBp. fronting the Ship Canal at Highfield. Another plot of land, 3r. 281 p., adjoining I it, was sold for £llO. Four cottages with gardens, 95 to 101, Halton-road, were disposed of for £340, and three others adjoining, numbered 103 to 107, were sold for £280.A block of cottages in Norton-st.,numbered 2 to 44, inclusive, and also a plot of land containing 3r, and a cottage at 49, Canal-st., were bid for by Mr. Jonathan Horsfield. who offered £l,BOO for them, but the lot was withdrawn. Two dwelling-houses, with out-buildings, schoolroom, yard and gardens, in Irwell-lane, were sold by private treaty after the sale. Messrs. Taylor, Kirk- ham, and Colley, were the solicitors for the sale. TRAP ACCIDENT. .

On Wednesday mci7r7;ia--;.-Cr—a-O—a-.ccident occurred in Lowland-road, in which Mr. Clement Handley, and Mr. H. Wesley-Cook sustained injuries. It appears that they were driving in a Gran belonging to Mrs. Stubbs, along Victoria-road, when the horse seemed to take fright and dashed onward. It succeeded in turning the corner at the end of the road and proceeded down Shaw-street, at a furious rate. When entering Lowland-road, the vehicle was overturned and the occupants thrown to the around. Both received injuries about the head and legs. Mr. William Darlington of the Railway Hotel, rendered prompt assistance and bandaged up their wounds. The horse received but slight injury and the only damage to the trap was the breaking of the splash board, It was very fortunate that at the time there were few persons n Shaw-street, or more serious consequences might have appened.

div.head: PROPOSED NEW CHURCH AT WESTON.
div.p: THE PROPOSED NEW CHURCH AT WESTON.
THE FETE AND SALE OF WORK.

Weston was undoubtedly en fête on Wednesday and Thursday when the Sale of Work and Village Fête was held. As is well known, the proceeds were in aid of the Weston Church building fund. For some time there has been a Dressing need for a church at Weston, and during the past twelve months efforts have been made to raise sufficient money to build one. A goodly sum has already been raised but still several hundred pounds are required to meet the entire cost. Elaborate preparations have been in progress for some time past with a view to mak- ing the Stle of Work and Fire an unqualified success. It was held at Cavendish Farm, kindly placed at the dis- posal of the committee by Mr. Thomas Ford. That the villagers took a great interest in the proc.edings was manifested by the great display of bunting. Out of , almost every cottage window there was protruding a flag of some description, and in some instances banners were stretched across the street. When Major Orred, who has taken a deep and practical interest in the pro- posal to erect a church at Weston, opened the sale and fête on Wednesday afternoon, the weather was threaten- ing, but fortunately it continued fine throughout the day, and added not a little to the success of the proceed- ings. The sale of work was held in one of the tents which had been erected in a field in close contiguity to the farm buildings. Here a number of stalls had been daintily set out with articles which come under that very inclusive phrase, "useful and ornamental." The Run- corn stall was in charge of Mrs. Maitland Wood, Mrs. R. Abel, Mrs. Whittaker and Mrs. White, and at the Weston stall there was in attendance, Mesdames Bankes,Mather, Guest, James Ford, jun., and Misses Armstrong, Bankes, E. Bankes, and Moss. Both of these stalls were laden with wearing apparel. In addition, there were the fol- lowing stalls in charge of the ladies mentioned below. The title of the stalls themselves, indicates clearly the goods that were on sale. Flower stall : Miss Pierpoint, and four flower girls representing spring, summer, autumn. and winter; toy stall, Mrs. McLennan, Miss F. Tim- mins,and Miss P.Tirnmins ; sweet stall, Miss Statham, Miss Stokes ; photograph stall, Miss Kenwright, Miss Mitcheson ; apron and pianofore stall, Miss of. Smith, Miss Crosby ; farm produce stall, Mesdames Signal, S Molyneux, Rogers, and J. Bankes. Occupying a tent to itself was the jumble stall, containing a medley of things which had become disused or not wanted by the large number of persons who had given them. In the refreshment and tea tents the following ladies were assisting :—Refreshments, Mrs.T. Ford with Mrs.Broad- hurst, Mrs. Halewood, Mrs. Poole, Mrs. J. Tudor, Miss Johnson, Mrs. Goddard ; tea tent, Misses A. Aaron, H. Basnett, Gregory, Farrah, Jones, Pendlebury, E. Tudor, and M. J. Tudor. There was a large company present at the opening ceremony. Major Orred was driven to the field in an open carriage, and was followed immediately behind by the Rev. Canon and Mrs. Wood. They were headed in their procession through Weston by the Church brass band, and on entering the field the band struck up, " See the conquering hero comes." Amongst those present in addition, there were :The Revs. W.H.Stables, 11. B. Firth, Fl. C. Moyle, D. S. Bowen, G. D. Wray, Messrs. C. L. Evans, J. B. Holland, Joseph Pritchard,J. J. Speakman, J. H. Weston, Thomas Ford, J. Ford, J. Joynson, J. Collier, E. Aaron, A. Guest, and others. In calling upon:Major Orred to open the proceedings,Canon Wood said he could not say his duty was to introduce Major Orred, because Weston knew him very well and respected him highly. He was the landlord of the town- ship of Weston, and was well known as a good landlord. That sale of work and fête was intended to help the building of the new church in Weston, and it was a matter of no little satisfaction to think that there was no kind of ill-feeling amongst members of any other Christian body in the village with regard to the building of that church. On the contrary they all wished them well. It might be asked, how was it that there was not a church at Weston ? He could only say that the Church of England was not a great big corpora- tion which possessed very large funds, and which it could distribute as it pleased. If it was such a corpora- tion many of the anomalies which existed would net be. There would not be a place like Weston with 1,200 in- habitants without a church. There were such places as Walton and Alvanley which had not more than a quarter that population, and yet they had a church and separate ministry belonging to it. But that was not the fault of the Church of England. They had no power to alter any of the funds which had been allotted by differ- ent people to different places. With regard to Weston, it had been different. It had been attached to the great parish of Runcorn, and therefore had not received the attention it otherwise would have done. In conclusion he referred to the generous way in which Major Orred had assisted the new church building fund.—Major Orred said he thanked them most heartily for the kind welcome they had given him, and he was only glad to do anything he could for the church at Weston. His father gave the land for the schools about 30 years ago, but the population had outgrown the Sin of the schools and a church was required. They,at•Weston, had helped themselves admirably and done marvellously well, and deserved every assistance they could get. He hoped they would receive it. He trusted the foundation of the new church would soon be laid, and then they could fire straight ahead. (Applause.)—A vote of thanks was ac- corded Major Orred for his presence that day, on the proposition of Mr. Thomas Ford, seconded by Mr. James Ford, and supported by Mr. Aaron. In acknowledging the vote, Major Orred, in alluding to what the speakers had said, re- marked that times had been hard for both landlords and tenants, bet if they worked together in .nutual con- fidenee, friendship, and good feeling, he believed they wculd succeed in the future as they had done in the past. The sale was then opened. A most important feature of the afternoon's proceed- ings was the crowning of the village queen, a grand march past, and presentation. About 100 people took part in the procession, and each represented some char- acter or other. A good number of those who partici- pated were frfein Riincorn. The chief characters were taken as follows :—Herald, Master Chris Imison ; Queen, Daiev Bakes ; Maids of Honour, Misses Gwennie Bushell and Fanny Price; Train Bearers, Misses Nora Jones,Elsie and Edith Robinson, and Marion Griffiths; Crown Bearer, Master Reggie Bankes ; Loris-in-Waiting, Masters Sidney Bankes, G. Palmer, G. Moores, It. Pad- bore ; Britannia. Miss Bertha McLean ; Ireland, Miss Emily Tudor; Wales, Miss S. Cameron. Numerous other characters were represented, even from Oliver Cromwell to niggers. Mr, Alfred Grounds made an inimitable girl of the future, whilst the girls of the past were represented by Misses Esther Farrel, Cissie Jones, Nellie Pendlebury, Alice Lightfoot, Alice Tudor, Florrie Millward. Misses Ida Kirkham, E. Handly, and M. Fla,ndley were flower girls; Miss J. Cameron, a nurse, Miss D. Cameron, a student, and two puritan maidens were represented be Miss EMMiff Bankes and Miss Arm- strong. Al ter marching past the thriine which had been erected in the field, the crowning of the village queen took place. Major OrriA performed the Pleasing duty, and during 'he ceremony the band played the National Anthem. Mrs. Ford handed to the young queen a beau- tiful bouquet, and the pronessionists were afterwards Presented to her. Maypole dancing was the next attrac- tion and this was done in an excellent manner by the following :—Henrietta Aaron, Flossie Pendlebury,Maggie MeMann, Bessie Rodgers, Annie Jones, Lottie Rogers, Jessie Anima, Sarah Oldfield, Maud Orme. Edith Scott, Mary Owen. Ethel McLean, Genie Bankes, Jessie Mather, Nellie Griffith, Maggie Bell, Lily Moores. They had been carefully trained by Miss Drinkwater. of Lostrnck, Miss Marlow, Mrs. Bankes, and Miss Arm- straw". O'her attractions were provided, including donkey races, cricket match (ladies v. gentlemen), and a concert in the evening. There was also a waxwork exhibition in charge of Miss Pierpnint. A new venture was the poultry. rabbit, bird, 'I and , flower show in which prizes were given for the best ex- Whits. Considering that it was the first show of the hind in Weston there was a good display by local amateur exhibitors. Appended is the list of the prize winners : POTTLTRY.—CIass 1, minorcas : 1, J. Dunbabin, Old Hall Farm, Wester. ' • very highly commended,Littlemore, Weston waterworks ; commended, Whitby, Weston Feint. Class 2. " Barn Door" : 1. J. E. C. Bankes, Weston ; 2. J. Dimbabin ; 3, Miss Ford, Manor farm, Weston; armlet prize' W. Bankes. High-st. • Runcorn ; v.h.c., J. E. C. Bankes; h.c., ditto. Chickens : 1, J. Dimbabin ; v he., W. Pendlebury. Gift class for the benefit of the funds ef the fete: 1, J. Jeffs, Weston ; 2, .T. Rank.% Weston Rouse; v.h.c., W. Pendlebury; c.. Miss Ford. Ducks ; 1, Miss Ford, v.h.c., J. Bankes. Snecial prize for Muscovy ducks, D. Kirkham, Weston Point. Eggs, hest dish of twelve s 1, J. Dunbabin, v.h.c., ditto ; v.h.c., John Griffiths, Weston Point ; c., J. Rankin. RABEITS.—Lops : 1, and 2, Samuel Edwards, 24, Cawdor-st.,,Runcorn ; 3, John Ward, 98, Church-street, Rlincorn v.h.c., ditto ; h.c., Samuel Edwards ; William Norton, Western. Dutch 1 and special. W. Bankes, Runcorn ; 2 and 3, S. Edwards, Run- corn: v.h.c. and reserve prize, Fletcher, 52, Union-st., Runcern. v.h.c., variety : 1, .1. E. Tweddell, Quarry Bank-terrace, Weston ; 2, W. Bankes, Runcorn ; h.c., William Charlesworth. Doe and litter : William Bankes, Hune,ern. A special prize for a guinea pig was awarded to Master T. Bankes. BIRD4.—York. canary : 1, Edward Rorie : 2, J.Clarke; 3, W. Davies. Norwich canary : 1 and 3, T. Mort ;2, H. Warburton; h c and c, Wheedan. Aspen. ; 2, J. Simian ; h e, J. Tudor. Cucumbers 1. and 2, W. Baxter. Cut blooms :1, G. Turner 2, G. Litiiemrirs. Some plants had been lent and others gived by the fol- lowing :—Messrs. Basnett. J. W. Listh,burn, W. Moores, A. Goorlier, and Littlemore. The officers for the fête were as Ninon. :—Chairman, Rev. Cam), Maitland Wood, M. A. ; treasurer, Messrs. A. Guest and T. T. sea ; ~,,ineral secretary, Rev. W. H. Stables 7 ami,tarv,3 assistant, Mr. J. Peacock ; secretary's messengers,
THINGS HEARD AND SEEN AT
RUNCORN.
BY OUR RTJNCORN CORRESPONDENT.

Sir John T. Brunner,L M.P., has this week pro- ceeded to Llandudno in quest of change and rest after his arduous labours of the past few weeks,and it is to be hoped that he will be greatly benefltted thereby. In a letter of thanks to the electors for again placing him at the head of the poll, he states that the Liberal party in the constituency had never been more united or more enthusiastic, and it had been an especial pride to him to have at his side so many of the old veterans with whom he worked in the old days of Mid-Cheshire. This was, no doubt,a most gratifying feature of the contest. The men- tioning of the old days of Mid-Cheshire recalls to mind how very different the result of that election was, as compared with that of the Northwich divi- sion of last week. The redistribution of seats, which gave Northwich one member, provided the Liberals with a far better chance of returning their candidate, and of this they have taken full advan- tage.

The Rev. Canon Wood recognises the hand of God in the overthrow of the late Liberal Government. As to what he would have thought, had the result been otherwise, he leaves us in doubt. But there is no doubt as to the former, for in his monthly letter to his parishioners he says " With regard to the elections I have only one thing to say and it is this, that whilst we recognise the hand of God in so providentially guiding the minds of the people of this country that Disestablishment has ceased to be a question of immediate concern, at the same time we are bound not to forget the prayer, which has gone up to [Ern from so many hearts, nor its full meaning. 0 Lord, we beseech Thee, let Thy con- tinual pity cleanse and defend Thy Church ; and because it cannot continue in safety without Thy succour, preserve it evermore by Thy help and goodness; through Jesus Christ, our Lord.' I wish, therefore, to suggest to you the continued use of this prayer, with the reminder that the cleansing of the Church should be as earnestly sought as its defence. Perhaps it should be added that it is always holiness which is its beat defence." It almost seemed that it would have been better if this latter reminder had been scattered broadcast for the benefit of zealous church defenders, prior to the election,and perhaps then we shonld have heard less of the alliance of beer and bible.

The building of a church at Weston bids fair to become an accomplished fact in the near future. The major portion of the money required is now in hand and it is to be hoped that as a result of the sale of work and fete which has been held this week, a substantial sum will be raised. The Wes- leyans it seems were the pioneers in the erection of a place:of worship in this township, which is becom- ing one of considerable size. In 1832, the Wes- leyans built their first chapel which was exchanged for a new one in 1831. In addition to this they have built a day and Sunday school. The Church of England built a day school in 1864,and in this services had been held ever since. Thus the Wesleyan have had a chapel in Weston for 63 years whilst the Church of England are still without a church.

The poor children of Runcorn will again be pro- vided with their annual treat this year. It is an event which is eagerly looked forward to by them, and it would be a great pity to discontinue it, des- pite the hard times which Runcorn people have ex- perienced. It must be remembered too that times have been far harder with the children for whom the treat is intended. It is well worth ths expen- diture which is entailed, and in a town like Run- corn there should be no great difficulty in raising sufficient funds.

div.head: HALTON PARISH COUNCIL MEETING.
div.p: HALTON PARISH COUNCIL MEETING.
THE CHARITIES.

The meeting of this Parish Council was held on Tues- day evening in the girls' schoolroom. The chair was oc- cupied by the Rev. G. 1). Wray, and there were also pre- sent Messrs. Looker, Hughes, Jeacock, Stokes, Barrow, Astbury, Ackerley, Reynolds, and McCulloch, and Mr. Woodier, clerk.

div.head: CHARITIES.
div.p: THE CHARITIES.

The Chairman gave the report of the Committee, con- sisting of himself, Mr. Looker, and Mr. Reynolds, ap- pointed at the last meeting to consider the trusteeship of , the Halton Parochial Charities. It said they met on the 22nd July, and in the consideration of the charities they bad taken Hadden's handbook on the Local Government , Act, as their guide. They found that parochial charities ; as regarded trustees, were of two classes, namely, those ; with more than one trustee,and those with a sole trustee ; It was explained that where there was no elective , element on the body of trustees of a non-ecclesiastica ; parochial charity, the Parish Council might appoint ad ditional members. They were simply permitted and not I required to make such appointment, and the number I was not to exceed what the Charity Commissioners ; allowed in each case. The Committee drew attention to this section, because there were charities which it might I be more convenient to leave in the hands of the present • trustees, if the Parish Council were satisfied that the charity was being properly administered, and was suffi- ciently safeguarded from loss. With regard to the Rev. 4 T. Alcock's school charity they found that nothing in 4 the Act should affect the trusteeship management or I control of any elementary school, an that this excluded the charity in Tiestion from the list of parochial chari- ties. As to Bolton's charity, it consisted of £657 23. Id. ; invested in 21 ner cent, of consolidated stock in the name of official trustees of charitable funds. It was originally invested in the names of Sir R. M. Brooke,the Rev. G. D. Wray, and Mr. C. L. Evans, who were the trustees at the present time for its administration. The charity was divided into three parts, one•third to St. Thomas' charity which was parochial under the Act ; one-third to the Vicar of Halton, which was ecclesias- tical, as defined namely "the endowment of which is held for the benefit of any spiritual person or ecclesias- tical officer as such " ; and one-third to the Halton Grammar School, which section 66 of the Act excluded from the list of parochial charities. The only portion i therefore with which they had to deal was the third belonging to St. Thomas' Day Charity. As the present , trustees wished to resign their position, the committee , recommended that application be made to the Charity Commissioners for permission for the Parish Council to appoint trustees in their place. With reference to Eaton's charity the trustee was Sir R. M. Brooke. This was divided equally between Halton Grammar school and St. Thomas' day charity, and it being under a sole trustee, they recommended that the Charity Commissioners be asked to approve of the number being increased to three. As the sole trustee had the power of appointing one, and the Parish Council the other, and as the former was desirous of it being under the management of the Parish Council, the committee recommended that the Council appoint one trustee and nominate another to be appointed by the sole trustee, and if the latter desired to resign, that the Charity Commissioners be asked to allow the Council to appoint the three. The Alms Rouse Charity they considered private. As to Stockham Charity the money was invested in the names of the official trustees. Formerly the trustees were Sir R. M. Brooke, the Rev. G. D. Wray, and Mr. C. L. Evans,who still administered It. Seeing that the help of the County Council and the Charity Commis- sioners appeared to be necessary before any alteration. could be effected the committee doubte the utility of altering the trusteeship if the parish meeting of Stock- ham and the ['Salton Council were satisfied that the Charity was pr r...erly administered and safeguarded from loss under the present trustees. They, therefore, suggested that it remain as at present. The st.Thomas' Day Charity belonged to the parish of Halton, and Sir R. M.l3rooke wiS the sole trustee for its administration. The deed provided that the money he distributed in such manner and proportion a,. should be thought fit by the minister,chapel wardens, and principal inhabitants. The committee applied the Na We remarks to this as to the Eaton Charity, as regarded the trusteeship. Weston Woodwall and Chesshyre Charity, the Rigby Charity, and the Halton Library the committee considered to be ecclesiastical charities. • MP Chairman gaive explanations respecting the various charities. He stated that with regard to the ! one for the widows of Stockham, a scheme to include Halton was forwarded to the Charity Commissioners, who also received an alternate one from the residents of Stockhana that it should be devoted to free
education. After consideration the former was ap- proved and accepted. —Mr. Jeacock said he

was not sure it was the wish of the Coun- cil to hinder Sir Richard Brooke from being a trustee,but rather that he would continue to occupy the position to act with one nominated by the Council.— Mr. Hughes trusted that Sir Richard would be given to understand that it was their desire that he would retain the position.—On the motion of Mr. McCullock,seconded by Mr. Stokes, the report was adopted, with the under- standing that the wishes of Sir Richard Brooke should be ascertained before the next meeting, when they could proceed with the nomination of trustees.

div.head: BURIAL BOARD.
div.p: THE BURIAL BOARD.

The Clerk reported that during the past month there had been four interments. The balance they had in hand was slightly over £2O. Mr. Wilson 11-id consented. to superintend the work in connection with the renova- tion of the cemetery wall, etc. The contracts were being propr-rly executed.—On the motion of Mr. Barrow second be Mr. Stokes, it was decided that the revision of the cemetery rules be submitted to a committee con- sisting of Messrs. McCullock, Hughes, and Jeacock.

div.head: PROPOSED CRICKET GROUND.
div.p: THE PROPOSED CRICKET GROUND.

The Chairman thought that before they went into a scheme for the above, the matter should come before a parish meeting. They had no right to increase the rates without their permission.—Mr. Stokes and Mr. Jeacock coincided, the latter remarking that they might carry out the suggestion by obtaining subscriptions.— Mr. Hughes thought that the subject would be met if a field could be rented which he was sure would be paid by those using it.—The Chairman promised to carry out the suggestion of Mr. Hughes, by seeing Sir Richard Brooke or his agent for the purpose of inducing them to place a field at their disposal.

div.head: YOUNG WOMAN'S SAD END. -- STOPPING OUT LATE AT NIGHT.
div.p: A YOUNG WOMAN'S SAD END. -- STOPPING OUT LATE AT NIGHT.

Mr. J. E. Worsley, coroner, conducted an inquiry at Runcorn Police Station on Tuesday afternoon, relative to the death of Gertrude Hindley, 16 years of age, daughter of James Hindley, mariner, residing at 65, York-st., Runcorn, who was found drowned in the Weston Canal on Wednesday evening. James Fiindley, father of the deceased, was the first witness called, and stated that the deceased was 16 years of age. On the previous Thursday night, the night on which there was a Liberal demonstration, he arrived home shortly before ten o'clock. He inquired where the deceased was, and was told that she was out. He had told her that she must be in at nine o'clock. He heard her come to the yard door and rattle it, at twenty minutes to eleven. He looked through the window and saw that it was her. He did not speak to her, and did not open the door to her because he had told her that he must be in at nine o'clock. Her mother went to the door about five minutes afterwards, bit deceased had gone. His object in not open- ing the door was to frighten her ; he never expected that she would go away. His wife tried to find her but was unable to do so. In answer to the Coroner, witness said that he did not tell deceased that if she was not in at nine o'clock he would lock her out. His boat was Iring at "accommodation lock "in the Weston Canal. It had been recently tarred, and de- ceased knew where it was lying. She had often been on board, and had slept on it once. But she must have known that the cabins were locked up. It was a very wet night, and it was raining when she rattlei the: back door of his house. In answer to a juryman as to how he knew it was his daughter that was at the gate, wit- ness said he saw her hat above the door. In answer:to another question he said he did not think it was his duty to go and look for the deceased ; when he bade them to be in the house at a certain time, he expected them:to be in. Another Juryman :It was an exceptional night? —Yes, but I was expecting her to stop at the yard door. —lnspector Hicks stated that on Monday, when the witness reported the girl missing, he asked him how he acc,unted for her running away, and he replied that it was in consequence of what her mother had said to her. Ann Hindley, mother of the deceased, deposed that she had told her several times to be in at nine o'clock, but she had not obeyed witness always. She stopped out rather late, and witness had remonstrated with her, and told her that she would fasten her out. When de- ceased had found the yard door fastened, she had gone round to the front door, and witness had et her in. On the night in question witness went to look for her but could not find her. She left the yard door open until nearly one o'clock, expecting her to come back. She was not a girl to sulk,and was not afraid to come home. Her father did not hit her ; she was a good girl. She thought that deceased would have gone to witness's sister, who lived in Arthur-st. She and deceased had slept there one night in a case of emergency. Witness did not know why the deceased went to the boat, and did not know how she came by her death.—By Mr. Shaw : Her hus- band had nc t beaten the girl lately P—No.—Didn't de- ceased arrive home about nine o'clock P—She first came in about 9 15, and asked witness to let her go out again and see the procession. Witness told her not to go fur- ther than the end of the street, and if she saw her father to Come home at once. In answer tea further question, witness said she did not know whether she told her husband of that occurrence when the de- ceased was knocking at the back door.. . . .

Mary Elizabeth Summerfield,7, Salishurv-streat,stated that she last saw the deceased alive at 10.30 on Thursday night. She seemed jolly enough when she left witness. Questioned by Inspector Hicks witness 6tated that she remembered having a conversation with the deceased about three weeks ago when she told witness that if anything befel her she would drown herself. Did you steow what she was alluding to ?—She had fallen out krtth her young man.—You understood her father was a wirn man P—Deceased told her that she had to be in by nine o'clock or her father would sauce her.

Mary Ann Dutton, 26, Lock-street, stated that she saw the deceased about a quarter past ten on Friday night last. She was standing near the Volunteer Drill Hall when witness was passing on the other side. Wit- ness would not have noticed her had deceased not asked her whether she was just going home. She was certain it was Friday night. James Boeg, waterman, stated that he recovered the body at a quarter past seven on Monday night from the Weston Canal. The body was opposite the stern of the vessel of which the deceased's father was captain. The body was floating. P.C. Gregory said from information received he went to the Weston Canal on Monday evening, and assisted to remove the body to the deceased's borne. He examined it and found a scratch on the left cheek and one on the right ear. There was gas-tar on the fingers and on the palms of the hands. The vessel had neen nes:. ly tarred and it appeared as if she had been trying to get on the vesiel. lhere• were no other marks about her. The scratch on the face might have been done by falling between the vessel and the stone lining of the canal.

The Coroner in summing tm said he thought they had' got the true history of this very sad and unhappy case. It appears that the girl had been in the habit of going out, it was not suggested that she had gone out for any improper or wrong purpose, but she had gone out against the wish of her parents from time to time. He did not think there had been any intention of lockiog her out, to keep her in the street all night. He believed that the girl -when she found the door locked, thought it would be better to see her father and mother next morn- ing. In his opinion she went to the boat and endeavoured to get on board and in doing so fell between the vessel and the wall of the canal, and was drowned. He thought there was only one verdict,and that was one of "Found drowned," to be returned in that case. With regard to the parents had they known what their action would be,they would never have done it. They believed they were giving de- ceased a salutary lesson. It was a very unfortunate termination, and it was a pity that the mother did not speak to her husband about the deceased having been in, and then afterwards gone to see the demonstration. The jury consulted together in private for a short time. P.C. Gregory was called into the room and read a letter which the police had received from a boatman named John Kursons, of Weston Point, who stated that on Thursday night his boat was lying near Weston locks, and he saw the deceased on the other side of the canal. She was near a vessel which was lying there. A verdict of " Folud drowned" was returned, and the jury exonerated the parents from all blame.

div.head: HALTON.
div.p: HALTON.

VISIT OF VoLuarrimas.—The Sergeants of the Ist Volunteer Battalion (Prince oi Wales) South Lancashire Regiment, Warrington, had their annual picnic to Helsby on Saturday. They visited their former instruc- tor, Sergeant Birch, at his hostelry, the Norton Arms Hotel, Halton. They had a main of bowls for several prizes, after which they partook of a substantial tea. Subsequently loyal and other toasts were honoured, in. eluding that of tha host and hostess. In responding to the latter, Mr. Birch heartily thanked the members of his corps for the kindly remembrance of him. They had come regularly during the past three years, and they might depend upon it that he would do all he possibly could for their happiness if they visited Halton in the future. The party left in waggonettes about 9.30 for home.
MERSEY GOLF CLUB.

Mr. Thomas Morris, F.G.S., who is vice presi- dent of the above Club, has presented for competi- tion to the members, a most unique timepiece,with silver-mounted Match stands as side pieces. The timepiece which is now on view in Messrs. W. Woods and Sons window, Sankey-at., is most suit- able and appropriate for the purpose. The articles used in this new popular game are placed round the base, whilst on the top is a figure of the golfer in the act of striking the ball.

The coroner's inquest relative to the death of Mrs. Coombes, w ife of a ship's steward, who was found mardered in her bedroom at Piaistow a fortnight ago, resulted on Monday in a verdict of wilful murder against the woman's two sans, the eldest a boy of thirteen.

Tim MUZZLING ORDER.—F. Parker, Cliffe View ; Ana Caldwell, and Peter Price were fined si. each for allow- ing their dugs to be at large nnmuzzled. Scaoot ATTENDANCE.—James Holland, of Cliffe View, for neglecting to cause his children to attend school regularly was fined 53. DRI7NIC ON LICENSED PREMISES.—Mr. Vickers was sum- moned for permitting drunkenness on his licensed premises, Main-street, Frodsham' on the 21st July, and William Corker was summoned for having been drunk on the licensed premises.—The evidence adduced by Sergt. Clays and P.C. Price was that at 9.20 on the date named (Sunday night), they visited the Volunteer Inn, kept by the defendant,Vickers. On going into the taproom they found Corker sitting asleep on a form. The atten- tion of the landlord was drawn to him and he was aroused. The landlord and his sou dragged Corker out of the house, and as soon as he get outside he fell down as if dead. He was very drunk. The landlord asked the police to make it as light as possible for him, and then he could get off with paying. The landlord also came to the Police Station on Monday,the 22ad, and said "Don't say any more than you can,it will be against me ; some Irishmen had been giving him drink. He was only served once from the time he came in." After further evidence the magistrates fined Vickers 103. and I.os.nosts, and Corker 24. 6 1. and Bs. 61. costs. AN ELECTION EPISODE.—John Challinor, and James Corker, Main-st., Frcdsham, summoned one another for assault. Corker admitted the offence but Challinor pleaded not guiltv.—Mr. A. Browne, Warrington, who represented Cballinor, stated that Corker, who was a Conservative, attended a Liberal meeting, held in sup- port of Mr. Roger Bate, the Liberal candidate for Eddie- bury, in Frodsham Town Hall on the 16th ult. Mr. J. M. Williams presided, and Sir John Bruaner addressed the meeting. The chairman told the audience that any question put in writing would be answered at the close of the meeting. Corker handed in two questions in different handwriting. One question was to the effect that Sir John 'Brunner introduced the eight hours' system into the works, and then asked the men to overwork their time, and in ine other question de- fendant asked if a single temperance reformer be- lieved that Sir William Harcourt's bill had helped for- ward the true solution of the temperance question. The chairman ruled that one question did not apply to the discussion, and he, therefore, refused to put it, and added that the other question would be answered by Mr. Bate on his arrival from another meeting. Corker, how- ever, was not satisfied, and kept interrupting the speaker till a Mr. Cleave, a Conservative, went to him, and tried to persuade him to go out. He refused, and interrupted the meeting again, whereupon the chairman requested some of the audience to eject him. Mr. Challinor and a few others then tried to put him out,but Corker got hold of a form, and clung to it. Eventually, the police were called in, and he was taken out. Mr. Challinor denied that be took defendant by the neck, and scratched him. On the following day—the polling day—Corker, in the presence of five or six witnesses, struck Challinor fiv or six times with his fist in the neck. Alt.r Mr. Challinor had taken out a summons a leading Conservative in Frodsham asked him to withdraw it. He refused, whereupon the Conserva- tive said it should not cost Corker a penny, as they would find all the money. The next morning a cross- summons was taken out by Corker. Corker, in making his complaint against Challinor, stated that he had handed in his questions, and the chairman told him he was out of order. Be (Corker) then addressed the meet- ing in a proper manner, saying " Mr. Chairman, and gentlemen, I wish to say lam not out of order." (Laught-r.) Cluillinor and four or five others wished to put him out, and " fine and rough " they were. ande. d seanortf, t(hLraolltgrlieltdeTh.?m,LstlearliticllhOirugs ehiizsednehcikm tdhi ed the election day he admitted he struck Challinor. Ele anybody to Challinor to try and settle the case. On was so excited about the way Challinor pulled him about • in the Town Hall that he could not help it. He (Corker) , denied that he continually interrupted the meeting. A nume.-e of witnesses were called on both sides,including Mr. Williams who spoke of the riotous manner Corker • conducted himself. It was through his howling and hassling that witness had to request his ejection.—The Bench fined Challinor 2s. 61. and Corker ss. ordering each to pay his own costs. The Chairman (Mr. Thomas added that Corker ought to have known better than attack Challinor the next day. P; was a great pity the cases had come there. They arose out of a political squabble, and it would have been far better if they had been settled outside.

div.p: BEFORE TH E MAGISTRATES.

CRITELTY TO ANIMALS—AN lIITERNSTING POINT. At the Warrington Borough Police Court on Friday, before Councillor H.Robert.s(chairman)and Mr.& Wright Thomas Price was charged with cruelly illtreating a horse by working the same on the 11th July when in an unfit state; and Thomas Burnard Kiernan landlord of the " Pattern Arms" was charged with causing the same to be worked.—Mr. C. H. Uusworth appeared for Mr. Kiernan who acct p'ed all respon*ibility in the matter.—P.C. Evans ste.ed that at 2.50 en the day in question he was in company with P.C. F. Monks and saw Price driving a bay mire attached to a cab. The mare was flinching and he examined the horse andturned up the saddle and found an Rld raw wound there about the size of a shilling, which was causing the horse great pain. There was also a slight wound on the off shoulder. He advised the driver •to take out the horse and not to work it. In company with Inspector Luff, B.S P.C.A. they later on visited the "Patten Arms" and found that some em- brocation had been applied to the wounds. They after- wards saw Mr. Kiernan who said he would take all responsibility in the matter.—P.C. Monks corroborated, and Inspector Luff said that the saddle of the harness had pressed directly unon the sore, and there was dried matter upon it.—Mr.Unsworth said it wage, paltry case which originated entirely through the malice of a dis- charged servant of Mr. Kiernan's. The police officer had admitted as much, though he would not give any name. Mr. Kiernan discharged this man a short time before' and he had in corFequence threatened to make it warm for him. In the second place,the Inspector would not wait for the appearance of Mr:Fergusson, veterinary surgeon, because Mr. Kernan had asked him peremp- torily to do so. Both Mr. Fergusson and Mr. Hewitt ha I examined the horse and he would call them.—Price, th driver, said the horse had been •flinching a little, but from what cause he did not know. Messrs. Fergusson and Hewitt deposed to having: ex- amined the mare on the date named, and found a small wound which would however not trouble the horse much unless pressed. Neither of them would hive been willing to work the horse.—Councillor Roberts said the Bench did not think it was a serious case. They did not like the manner in which the information had originally been conveyed and did not wish to encourage that practice.—They fined Mr. Kiernan in the costs in both cases.

FRlDAY.—Before Councillor U. Rooerts (chairman), and
Mr. S. Wright.

FACTORY ACT PROSE-C—GTI-0-N.Leharles Henry Bennett, baker, 53. Bewsey-street, was charged with having on the 29th July, he being the occupier of a workshop in the meaning of the Act, failed to give notice to the Inspector as required by the Act within a month of commence- ment.—Mr. James Henry Rogers, H.M. Inspector of Factories, stated that defendant was the occupier of a bakehouse in Bewsey-street and be had neglected to send the notice of commencement el work within one month. , It seemed that early in this year, some five or six months ago, Mr. Bennett commenced the business and had not yet sent any notice. His (the Inspector's) assistant had visited defendant in Bewsey-s,reet on the 26th June, 29th June, and sth July, in the first two eases giving, word to Mrs. Bennett of the necessity for notice and in the third to Mr. Bennett. They had been almost unduly lenient in this case as they were not b )und to caution any occupier.— Ambrose Thomas, inspector,said he had visited the defendant and wife on the occasion named and mentioned the matter. lie corroborated his super- ier.—The Chairman thought the Department had acted with very great considers tien in this case and they would fine defendant in the costs (104.) AN ELECTION QUARREL.—Ana Brown and Annie Speak- man, 58, Lythgoes-lane, were charged with assaulting Amy Hayes on the 21st July. Mr. Browne represented defendants and alleged provocation for the assault.—The magistrates dismissed the case as a paltry one. USING THREATS.—Thomas Stone, 80 Winwick-st., was ' charged with using threats to Thomas S 1an,49 Tanner's- lane, on the 23rd July.—Mr. Browns represented zom- ' plainant and stated that defendant pulled out a knife to complainant.—The Bench hound defendant over to keep the peace in his own recognizances. PALTRY ASSAULTS —William Bibby, 41 Chorley-sl...was charged with assaulting Gilbert Gleave and Dinah Gleave on the 19th July; Dinah Gleave was charged with assaulting Bibby.—Mr. Forshaw prosecuted. The reve- lations made showed that there was not much to choose between both parties, and the magistrates characterizing the case as a disgraceful one ordered each party to pay ilits own costs.—Alfred Garnett, Gee-st., was dismissed on a charge of assaulting and beating Amy Ford on the 15th July.—Fanny Brocklehurst was similarly treated for a like charge of assaulting Margaret Kelly on the 18th inst. A REPENTANT TIIIEF.—James Taylor, a man with a bad character,was charged with stealing from the Model Lodging House, Friar's Green, on 2nd July, a cash box containing 83. 21., the money of Alfred Brouchemite.— Mr. Hunt stated that the office door of the lodging-house was discovered burst open and the money gone. Mr. Hunt had received a telegram from Manchester stating that prisoner had surrendered himself there and con- fessed the theft. Detective Monaghan went over and received him in custody.—Prisoner was sent o gaol for three months' hard labour.
SATURDAY.—Before Mr. John Biimess (chairman), and Mr. S. Chandley._ .

DRUNK AND DISORDSMLY.—Martin Hart was chaetted with being drunk and disorderly in Friars' Green at 1/.5 on Friday night. It appear; that he was intoxicated and had been using obscene language and threats. The magistrates fined him 101. and costs or 14 days' hard labour. MONDAY.—Before the Mayor (chairman). Alderman Francomb, Mr. F. Monks, and Mr. J. W. Hayward. DRUNKENNESS.—For this offence committed in Bank. street, an Sunslay night, John and Ellen Smith, were committed to gaol for one month ; Jane Mather, in Euttermarket-street, on July 17, 103. and costs or 14 days; John and Hannah Conway. 6, Robinson's-yard, Fennell-st., in Fennell-st., on July 20, the former sent to gaol for one month, and the latter discharged ; Daniel Hennessey, 5, Cropper's-brow. on July 20, in Cropper's- brow 53. ; Michael Quinn, 6, Berry's-yard, on Jul % 20, in Tanner's-lane, Si. and cost., or seven days ; Charles Stewart. Pinner's-brow. on July 22, Si. and costs. UNLICENSED DOG.—For keeping dog without a license, Henry Gregg, 8, Back Lord-street, Latchford, was fined ss. AR INSUFFICIENTLY MUZZLED MM.—James Marsh, 116, Pierpoint-at., was fined 10s. for this offence. The dog had bitten a little girl although it had a muzzle on. This is the first case of this character which has been brought before the magistrates in Warrington, RIDING " BARE-BACICED."— A. boy named William Hickins, 14, Ellen-st., was charged with furiously driv- ing a pony in Hoyle-street, on July 20.—P.C. Chrimes said that he saw the lad on the pony's back going at a high rate of speed in the direction of Folly-lane. The pony had neither bridle, saddle, or halter, and was being ridden bare-backed. He had got upon the pony's back in Hoyle-street, for a ride, but when he had got on, the pony started off at a gallop, and the boy could not get off again.—ln reply to the magistrates, the defendant said that he was not used to horses,and he did not know to whom the pony belonged.—Alderman Francomb ob- served that the defendant must be another Fred Archer n being able to ride a pine hare-backe.l.—The Benchi eci dad to let the &lead I;it Off on the, pvsent occasion h a dats of 13.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, AUGUST 3, 1895.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, AUGUST 3, 1895.

FOOTBALL PLAYING IN THE STREET.—SaMIIeI Baines and William Lawless, both oi 46, Buttermarket-st., were each fined ss. and costs for playing, football in Friars'- green on Sunday, July 21.—P.C.'s Barlow and Sankey proved the case. CHIMNEY ON FlRE.—William Emison, Market-street, was fined 11. and costs for allowing his chimney to be on fire on July 22. TUEsDAY.—Before Mr. R. Garnett (chairman), Councillor H. Roberts, and Dr. T. Starkey Smith. TEMPORARY AIITHORITY.—Georue Parr was granted temporary authority to sell as an off-license in School-at., in lieu ot Caroline Scales.

WIDNESDAY.—Before Mr. J. Geddes (chairman), Mr. J. H. Fleming and Mr. John Faircdough. ABSENTING HIMSELF FROM TRAINING.—John Mallett was remanded to await escort for absenting himself from the annual training in the Third Lancashire Militia on July 10. Sergeant Gilbert said that be recognised the. prisoner as being one of his own regiment. P.C. Gibbs, who arrested the prisoner, was recommended for the usual reward.

THEFT OF IRON HURDLES—Richard Boscow, 26, Old Gardens, was charged with stealing five iron hurdles,the property of John Mainwaring, auctioneer, • the.previous day. The Chief Constable said that the complainant held periodical sales at the Eagle and Child yard,Bridge- street, and on Tuesday, .Detective Monaghan received information that some iron hurdles had been stolen from the yard. He subsequently discovered that they had been sold to James 'Foote, Allen-street, by the defendant. Monaghan searched for,the defendant during the day, but towards evening, the latter came to the police station and gave himself up, admitting the theft. The magis- trates sent the defendant to gaol for 14 days, and expiessed dissatisfaction that Mr. Toole had not made more inquiries before purchasing the hurdles. THCIRSDAY.—Before Mr. S. Chandley (chairman), Alder- man Sutton, and the Mayor. A VISITOR ON THE SPREE—Peter Riley, 15 Waston- street, Birkenhead, was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Buttermarket-street at 8.15 on Wednesday night ; he was further charged with assaulting P.C. Hot- lingworth at the same time and place.—Be pleaded guilty to both charges —P.C. Bolling worth said that on the night in question he saw prisoner drunk in Butter- market-street and using foul language. Prisoner fol- lowed him to Market Gate, after being advised to go to his lodgings, and there attacked him breaking his whistle chain. They had a short struggle and prisoner was ul- timately bought to the Police Station and locked up.— The magistrates fined prisoner 10s. and coats for the off- ences, but as he had only Bs. upon him he was allowed to leave the town on paying that sum.
NEWTON PETIT SES'SIONS.
SATURDAY.—Before Mr. T. J. G,llepTie (chairman: Colonel J. L. Wood, and Mr. S. S. Brown.

CRUELTY TO ANIMALS.—Peter Lannigan was charged with working a horse while in an unfit state at Newton on July 20th. Inspector Luff, R.S.P.C.A., said that on the above date he was outside Newton race course, and noticed the defendant driving a bay gelding attached to a waggonette. The animal was flinching, and upon examining it, wi'ness found an old raw wound which the collar was chafing, and out of which blood was being discharged. The defendant said that he had brought eight passengers from Widnes, and the horse belonged to James H. Lee.—The magistrates inflicted a fine of 7s. 6d. and costs and expressed the hope that the master would pay the fine.—James H. Lee Mired King and Robert Williams, all of Widnes, were charged with causing a horse to be worked while in an unfit state on July 20th. Mr. J. W. Knowles defended. Inspector Luff said that Lee was a cab proprietor in Widnes, King was his manager, and Williams the stable man. The animal in question was the one for which the last defen- dant had been fined. Evidence of corroboration was ...liven by Sergeant Barnes.—Peter Lannigan, the driver of the horse, said that he told the ostler that the horse had got a sore shoulder and he did not want to get locked up.—The magistrates were then invited to see the horse which was brought below for them to see it, and upon their return they dismissed the case. DRUNKENNESS.—Ann Foyle, Newton, was fined 24. 6d. costs for this offence; Edward and John Coyne, Newton 2s. 6d. and costs ; Patrick Ryan, Newton, 6s. and coats; Benjamin Wadsworth, Flaydock, 2s. 6d. and costs; John Dwyre, Havdock, 2s. 6d. and costs; William Corfield, Havdock, 2s. 6t and costs. DOGS AT LARGE.—For allowing their dogs to be at large unmuzzled, Josiah Cuthbert Atkinson Earlestown, was fined 34. 6d. : John Chesworth,. Haydoclr, 3i. 61.

, „ PLAYING PITCH AND Toss.—For playing piton and LOSS in Newton on July 19, Joseph Gallaghan was fined Is. and costs.—Thotnas Glover and Frank Hitchin were fined is. and costs, for the same offence committed in Gl'borne, on June 19. A MILICSELLER SuNatoNeo.—George Howarth, milk- seller, Earlestown, was summoned for selling to James I Parkinson, on July Ist, a pint of new milk which was not of sufficient quality. James Parkinson who was an inspector of the Royal Agricultural Society, said that he sent a portion of the milk to the county analyst, who had certified that it contained 313 parts out of 100 of fat, 7.81 other solids, making a total of 10 85 solids. There were also nine parts of water. In reply to Mr. R. Stuart who defended, Mr. Parkinson said that he was not a chemist, and could not tell how much solids it was necessary for milk to contain.—lt was finally decided to adjourn the case until the next sessions day. A QUARREL —James Chadwick was charged with as- saulting and beating Henry Crowther, on July 22nd, at Newton. The complainant said that he was at the Griffin Hotel on the day in question, and while there the defendant came and "took a running kick "at him, and hurt him in the thigh. He could give no cause for this behaviour, unless it was because he was of a differ- ent colour in politics. The defendant said that he was aggravated by the complainant. He denied kicking him but said that he simply pushed him.—Defendant was bound over for six months. OVERDRIVING HORSES —Richard Bailey was charged with driving a horse at Newton on July 19th. Inspector Luff said that the horse had been used for bringing pas- sengers to Newton race course, and was in a very poor condition. It was breathing very heavily when witness saw it owing to being- over driven. Defendant was fined 20s. and costs for committing a similar offence on July 24, at Newton. Inspector Luff and Sergeant Barnes pr,ved the case. " CAUGHT IN THE ACT."—John Smith, 26, Marshall-Bt. Leda. was charged with attemp.ing to steal a watch from the person of John Garrity, Church-st., Golborne, at Newton Races,on the previous Saturday. Complain- ant stated that he was on the racecourse on the clay named,when he felt a slight tugging at his watch chain. Be turned sharply round and saw the prisoner with his hand taking the watch from the chain. He caught him in the act, and held him until the police came to his assistance.—Prisoner, who had nothing to say, was sent to orison for 21 days hard labour.

-- - THEFT OFA SHIRT --Edward Edmondson was charged with having stolen a hirt,value 4s. 6d., the property of Samuel Arrowsmith, Church-st., Golborne, on the pre- vious day. Complainant stated that the prisoner had been staving at his house for two or three nights, and on the day in question the shirt was missed. Information was given to the police.who ascertained that the prisoner had attempted to pledge the shirt. He was, however. detained and given into'custody.—Prisoner.who pleaded that he was drunk at the time, was sent to gaol for 21 days, with hard labour.

DRUNICENNESS.—WiIIiam Douglas, a coloured man, was fined ss. including costs for being drunk at Waterloo Bridge on the 27th July.—John Forbes was mulcted in a similar penalty for a like offence on the 28th ult.—P.C. Butler proved both cases. BRUTAL ASSAULT ON HIS WlFE.—Thonsas Gandy, waterman, St. John-street, was charged with having on the 10th June at Runcorn, unlawfully and maliciously wounded his wife, Ellen Gandy.—The prisoner's wife stated that on Monday the 10th June, the prisoner came home abont 330 in the afternoon under the influence of drink. He had been drinking all the week previous. He beat her with the fire-tongs and also kicked her. Had it not been for neighbours, she did not think he would , have done it. Whilst on the ground he struck her on ' the mouth and then kicked her. She was knocked senseless and did not know how many times he struck her. Two of her teeth were knocked out and others broken. She took out a warrant against him, but he had been away ever since.—lnspector Hicks stated that on the date named the previous witness came to the police station. She could scarcely speak, and her teeth were half-in, and half-out. Her lip was cut right through by the teeth, and was a most ugly gash. She told him that her husband had hit her with the tongs. and kicked her. A warrant was issued. On visiting the house he found blood on tha fireplace and on the floor. It looked more like a slaughter-house. Ile man absconded the same day.—The prisoner stated that he was drunk at the time. He hoped the magistrates would be lenient with him and he would see that it did got hempen again. He had been drinking heavily the week before he assaulted his wife. He could not keep the beer down and he took some spirits which made him worse. He was committed to gaol for three months' hard labour. '

WARRINGTON T. MANCHESTER (BATES AND CLARK'S BENEFIT). —The return match between these clubs was played at Arpley on Saturday. the game being set apart for the benefit of the two professionals, Bates and Clark. A hearty response was made to the appeal, and an at- tendance was recorded of considerably over two thou- sand persons. Some sensational cricket was witnessed, and although rain fell heavily at times during the after- noon, the sport was thoroughly enjoyed. The feature of the match was the sound innings of Dr. R. Smith for Warrington, and the brilliant bitting of Baker and Mr. A. C. Maclaren, who, whilst they were associated, pot together no fewer than 151 runs,and almost pulled off a victory for the Mancunians. The wicket was easy throughout the afternoon, and the batsmen had a dis- tinct advantage, for with the repeated showers the bowlers were handicapped in having to perform with a wet ball. div.head: RUNCORN PETTY SESSIONS
div.p: RUNCORN PETTY SESSIONS

MONDAL—Before Mr. C. Hazlehurst and Mr. Thomas Handley. Does AT Lsces.—Margaret Carney, fiBl4clsalsr, was summoned for allowing a dog to be at lame in High- street, Runcorn, on the 17th July.—Samuel Fester, was summoned for a similar offence in Halton-road on the 21st July.—Both defendants were fined 51. including costs.

TRANSFER OF LlCENSEs.—Williani Parr anplied for an occasional license to sell at the Queen's Head beerhouse, High-street, lately occupied by William Deeprose ; and Joseph Baker, of Warrington, applied for permission to sell at the George Inn, Poole-lane, previously occupied by Andrew Walker—Both applications were granted. DAMAGING A DOOR.—Mary Hulse, 8, Loch-street, was summoned for wilful damage to a door by break- ing two panels at the house occupied by Phcehe Price. Loch-street, doing elama.Te to the extent of 133. 61.—The complainant, Mrs. Price, stated that on the previous Monday afternoon, the defendant who was the worse for drink, came to her house and kicked the door until two of the panels were smashed in.—Corroborative evidence was given by Mrs. Hall, a neighbour.---The defendant whilst admitting that she kicked the door, denied the extent of the damage. A joiner who had examined it had told her that there was net above three- pennyworth of damage done. She had received great provocation from the ccmplainant.—The magistrates fined her 255. including costs, or in default, 14 days' imprisonment. AN EtzertoN ErisODE.—Mary Ann Glover was charred with having on the 24th July assaulted Elizabeth Taylor. It appeared from the evidence of the complainant that on the date named, which was election day, she was in the shop of Messrs. Speakman Bros., chemists, when the defendant came in, wearing a hunch of yellow flowers. The complainant told tier that she had got the wrong colour in her breast whereupon the defendant pulled the red ribbon out of the complainant's hat, tore it in shreds, and trampled upon it in the street, using had language at the same time. The complainant waited in the shop for a short time, hut on coming out she was met by the defendant who struck her in the eye. —Margaret Bowden gave corroborative evidence.—.?C Gregory gave corroborative evidence as to seeing the blow struck by the defendant. He did not know what the bother was about.—The defendant's version of the affair was that the complainant on seeing her enter the shop, accosted her with the words, " We are going to have no Home Rule here," and then nulled out the yel- low flowers defendant was wearinF!,throwingthem to the ground. She admitted pulling the red ribbon from out ' of complainant's hat, but with regard to striking her,sbe said it was done in self defence, as the complainant first pushed her over some potatoes outside Mr. Kirkham's shop.—The magistra,es considered the case oroved and fined her in the costs, 7s. 81.' or in default 14 days' im- prisonment. On leaving the dock she raid she would do fourteen days, and would do fourtefn more for the com- plainant wbert gbe came out.
