div.head: DARESBURY PETTY SESSIONS.
div.p: DARESBURY PETTY SESSIONS.

TUESDAY.—Before Messrs. William Long in the chair), Mclntyre, and H. Neild. DRUNKENNESS. Caleb Skidmore, for having been drunk whilst in charge of a horse and carriage, on the 30th June, at Appleton, was fined 103. including costs. —For having been drunk and riotous,the following per- sons were fined in the sums stated :—Esther Clayton Appleton, 2s. 6d., including costs ; and Patrick Casey Walton, 53. including costs. Fuatous DRIVING.—A fine of 23. 6d. including costs, was inflicted upon Alfred Henry Arnold, for having furiously driven two horses attached to a dray, on the 13th inst., at Moore. SETTING THE SANITARY AUTHORITY AT DEFIANCE.— John Bostock, builder, of Appleton, was charged at the instance of the Runcorn Rural District Council with having on the 11th June, at Appleton, pulled down a plate, on which was the name of a street, and which had been placed on his (defendant's),house by order ot the Council. —William Bostock, father of John Bostock, was charged with aiding and abetting the said. John Bostock in the same charge.—Mr. Arthur Browne ap- peared for the defendant and pleaded guilty.—Mr. Ash- ton, clerk to the Runcorn District Council said that a plate, on which were the words "London-road," had I been placed at the end of the defendant's house by the Rural District Council, and,on the day mentioned in the charge, John Bostock pulled it down,and threw it away, being instructed to do so by his father, William who seemed to set the Authority at defiance. He (Mr. Alton would like a penalty inflicted, just to let Mr. Bostock know that be could not do just as he liked.—Mr.Browne stated that the defendants had removed the plate be- cause they wanted it on the garden wall,and not on the end of the house. They did not know there was any harm in doing so, and had offered to replace the plate if it was given to them by the Runcorn Rural Council. —The Bench imposed upon William Bostock a fine of 2s. 61 and costs, whilst the case against John Bostock was dismissed, as he had only acted on his father's in structi on,

CRUELTY TO A HORSE.—Peter Johnson was charged with having cruelly illtreated a horse, on the 24th of June, at Moore.—Witnessas were called, whose evidence went to prove that the defendant was seen to throw large stones at the horse, which he was working in a field. —Defendant said that he expected rain, and wanted to get the hay in. He did not do it to hurt the animal.— Defendant was fined 2s. 6d. including costs. ANGLERS IN Thooacx —John Bennett and Arthur Willett were charged with having on the 22nd July, at Streeton, been found angling in prohibited waters, on property belonging to the trustees of Peter Leather.— Mr. Knowles (instructed by Messrs. Davies, Kirkconnel, and Davies) prosecuted, and said that the defendants had been previously warned off the land by the tenant, Mr. Benshall. In getting to the pond, which contained a large number of fish, the defendants had crossed a field of oats, and had done much damage.—Defendants, who denied that Mr. Henshall had previously warned them, were each fined 5s including costs. AN UNPROVOKED ASSAULT.—Henry Sandhurst was charged with having on the 21st inst., at Whitley, assaulted Frank Bell.—Complainant stated that he was ' leaving the Chetwode Arms on the day named at about 230 p.m., when he met the defendant. The latter, without the least provocation, ran towards him and struck him in the mouth, cutting his lip. Defendant also struck him another blow behind the neck.—Sand- burst, who pleaded guilty and said that the complain- ant had been scandalising his name, was fined 2s. 6d. and costs. TRESPASSING IN SEARCH OF GAME.—Frank Beach and Peter Corley were charged with having been found trespassing on certain land at Preston Brook, in search of game, on the 23rd June.—Jonathan Shepley, game- keeper, said that he, with another keeper named Williams, was watching the defendants on the day in question about three a.m., and saw them fire guns at game. When the defendants saw witness and his com- panion. Beach turned round and threatened to shoot. Williams, however, recognised the two men, and accord- ingly procured a trap and drove to Barnton, where the assistance of a police-sergeant was secured. The thregi men then went to the house occupied by the defendants, but were not able to see them. The defendants had kept out of the way for three or four days,but were at length apprehended. Defendants pleaded not guilty, and said that they were in bed at the time stated.—Beach was fined 10s. and costs, and Corley 20s. and costs.

div.head: HALE SEPTUAGENARIAN.
div.p: A HALE SEPTUAGENARIAN.

It is unnecessary to go back to the Greeks or Romans to find examples of vigorous old age. Great Britain fur- nishes numerous instances of this prolonged vitality and supremacy of will, which successfully resists the per- petual dragging back to the original physical weakness from which mankind from infancy emerges. The world pays homage to well-preserved monuments of the past— hale and hearty beyond the alloted three score years and ten—with intellectiial, spiritual, and physical force which shows no signs of the ravages of time, and is glad to catch an occasional glimpse from their inner private lite, which may show how health, vigour, and strength are best sustained and prolonged. We shall never for- get the words of Miss Ann Dickson, 61, Lothian-street Edinburgh, as contained in a recent letter received from her: " I am a septuagenarian whose brain is active, and who inherits a temperament which—although not un- wholesomely nervous—may perhaps be best tabulated as 'nervous-bilious.' Past and present experience of the efficacy of Warner's Safe Remedies ensure thoughtful- ness with tespect to the necessity of keeping Warner's Safe Cure and Warner's Safe Pills always near me, and I fef I very grateful for the salutary and beneficial effects derived from their use."

div.head: LATE COLONEL McCORQUODALE.
div.p: THE LATE COLONEL McCORQUODALE.
MAGISTERIAL REFERENCES AT NEWTON.

At the Newton Petty Sessions on Saturday morning, Mr. T. J. Gillespie, the Chairman of the Bench said that before proceeding to the business of the court, it was with deep sorrow he had to refer to the death of their late chairman, Colonel McCorquodale. Colonel McCor- quodale was ore of the senior members of the West Derby Hundred, and for 36 years he had been a magis- trate, and had attended that court. In fact, he had at- tended most regularly, sad he (Mr.. Gillespie) had known him come at great inconvenience, even from Scotland in order to attend the court on Saturday morn- ing. The interest he took in the business of the court, the care and the anxiety he showed in having every case thoroughly at his fingers' ends,before giving his de- cision, and his regularity in attending the court, left an example which it would be well for the justices of that division to follow. As regarded his private life, he (Mr. Gillespie) could speak with authority. For over 40 years he had Lnown the Colonel intimately, and his genial and hearty manner he would never forget. He regretted I Colonel McCorquodale's loss most sincerely,and he knew he was only giving voice to the sentiments of everyone in that court wEen he expressed to Mrs. McCorquodale his very deepest sympathy in her heavy bereavement. Mr. Henry Greenall (magistrates' clerk), said that he agreed with every word which had fallen from Mr. Gillespie. He haillenown Colonel McCorquodale for thel whole of his life and had always received the greatest kindness from him. There was no magistrate on the bench who gave greater care to the cases which came before him. Mr. R. Stuart, solicitor, joined heartily in the expres-1 Mons of sympathy and regret at the death of Colonel I McCorquodale. He was a man universally beloved and he always did all that it was possible, to do justice and right to all who came before him. Mr. J. W. Knowles, solicitor, also expressed his regret and sorrow at the death of Colonel McCorquodale. He had known the Colonel for many years, and his conduct on the bench was most gentlemanly and dignified. and he must say that that court was one of the most digni- fied and well-conducted courts that he knew of in the county, and that was without doubt in a great measure due to the conduct of the late Colonel McCorquodale. Superintendent Hig,ginbottom, on behalf of the police, endorsed all that had been said by the previous speakers. He said that the police had lost a good and sincere friend.
The business of the court was then proceeded with.

div.head: BOWLING.
div.p: BOWLING.
SARACEN'S HEAD v. WINNINGTON PARK.

A. match between these two clubs was played on Saturday at Winnington. The Saracen's Head team were driven in two conveyances,the route lying through a pleasant country. They met with a cordial welcome at the hands of their opponents, and the contest proved a most enjoyable one. The green forms a part of the Splendid recreation grounds provided by Messrs. Brun- ner, Mond and Co., for the benefit of their workpeople. The grounds include two bowling greens, a cricket ground, lawn tennis courts, and a bicycle track. They were all in fine condition and were greatly admired by the visitors. The home team were captained by Mr. R. Nocrass, and the Saracen's Head team by Mr. H. Fogg. Double and single games were played, the former being 13 up and the latter 11 up. As will be seen from the scores, the visitors only -succeeded in winning two games in the doubles and three in the singles, and in the end they were defeated by 85 points-60 on the doubles and 25 on the singles. As this was the first match, the Saracen's Head team are looking forward to the return match at Wilderspool in the hope of being able to reverse the position of affairs. At the close of the match, the visitors and several of the home team had tea together at the Stanley Arms, Mr. H. Fogg and Mr. T. Ince (secretary) afterwards expressing the gratification of the team at the reception they had had. Mr. Lockwood replied on behalf of the home team. A start for home was naade about half-past eight, and was reached shortly before ten, all the bowlers being highly pleased with the outing. Scores : SARACEN'S HEAD. WINNINGTON PARK. div.head: GANG OF FORGERS.
div.p: A GANG OF FORGERS.

A dangerous set of criminals has been removed from the midst of society for a time by the conviction of the three men charged with forging letters of credit on Messrs. Coutts and Co. They were brought up for sent- ence at the Old Bailey on Tuesday morning. It was shown that they had all been concerned in band rob- beries and serious commercial frauds, and one of them, John Carr, a man of 67, was described as chief of a ,tang of most expert Continental forgers and thieves, and as a person possessed of a considerable amount of property. Mr. Justice Collins sentenced Carr to six years' penal servitude and ordered that he should pay the costs of his prosecution, and the other prisoners were sentenced to eight and ten years' penal servitude.

GREAT SANKEY &Hoot. Boann.—The monthly meet- ing of this body should have been held on Tuesday afternoon. Only Mr. W. P. Skelton (chairman) and Mr. H. Bate, however, appeared as members of the Beard, so that a quorum was not formed. Mr. W. D. Jeans, clerk, was also present. The report issued by the master of the school (Mr. George Clarke l stated I that for the week ending July 20th the number of scholars on the school's books was 366, 333 of whom were present, producing an average attendance of 288.3. For the following week 369 were on the books; 346 were present ; the average attendance being 2937. Continuing the master observes :—The attendance has been very low during the past two weeks. The Atten- dance Officer has warned those children who have had very bad attendance. The numbers to-day are higher."

div.head: IRON TRADE.
div.p: THE IRON TRADE.

There is not much movement in the iron trade just now. New business is rather scarce, but manufacturers are for the most part well employed on old orders, and hopeful as to the future. Some good contracts for con- structional work for India and the colonies have been secured lately by local engineers, and these represent in the aggregate a considerable tonnage of iron and steel. The principle demand at present is for black sheets for galvanizing, which are strong at about 23. 61. advance on last quarter's average. Strip-makers report an improved demand from tube manufac- turers, but business in bar iron is rather languid, and prices for this class of iron relatively weak. Midland pig is in good demand, and prices in this department are steady. S affordshire pig is 50s. to 525. 6d. for all-mine, and 395. to 403. for part-mine ; cinckr is 343. 6d. to 355. Northamptonshire forge is 389., North Staffordshire 403. 6d. to 42i., Derbyshire 393. to 405., Lincolnshire 41s. to 425., and hematite 51s. to 523. Makers of marked bars report business quiet, at £7 to £7 12s. 6d. Merchant iron is £5 103. to £6. Common bars are £5 23. 6d. to £5 ss. Shects are £6 12s. 61., and in some cases £6 153. for doubles, and £7 to £7 ss. for lattens. Plates are £6 10s., angles £5 12g. 81., stamping sheets, £7 103., and best thin sheets £lO. Hoop and thin strip are £6 ss. Nailrod is £6 , 103., and tube strip £5 ss. Steel is steady at about £4. , for Bessemer billets and blooms, £5 ss. to £5 10a. for ' angles, £5 10s, for tank-plates, and £5 153. to £6 for bars, Galvanised iron is still quoted 17s. 6d. to £lO in Liverpool for 24g. North Staffordshire bars are quoted £5 2s. 61., 'angles £5 12s. 61., and hoop-iron in Liverpool £5 15s.

div.p: 'lto

CANVASSING. Sir,—l was interested in reading last Saturday the letters on this question, and I would like to add if you .will permit me that canvassers who are over anxious about their party might be tempted if they met a care- less voter to offer him a drink to plump for their party.l think canvassing ought to be done away with so as to save temptation on both sides. I should also like to hear of the secrecy of the ballot being made entirely free from conjecture and suspicion. Conveyances should I think, only be used for the aged and cripples.—Yours truly, A READER.

div.head: WARRINGTON M ARKET.
div.p: WARRINGTON M ARKET.

Sir,—Allow me to congratulate the Markets Com- mittee upon the stand they have taken at last to open a wholesale market. As the placards don't clearly define who and what are the wholesale &al Ars, I hope it will be very sweeping in effect. While strongly in favour of giving every encouragement bra wholesale market con- ducted the same as others throughout the country, I strongly condemn the principle it has been carried on in the past, namely, to the hurt of those stall holders who have to pay from six shillings to twenty shillings per week, besides gas, &c., which accumulate to a heavy sum, and then have to compete with those who only pay one penny per article, hamper or bag, styled as country growers but in reality only cottage commission agents for their neighbours. These people and these alone have first preference over old standards, and then after supplying wholesale commence to retail out at prices the alaove ratepayers have to compete with and as a result are reduced almost to poverty through the en- couragement given to such unjust competition. Seeing our Markets Committee claim theirsto be the best paying concern we have, showing a nett profit on the past year of £2,388, I trust our respected market inspectors will do their uttermost to remedy the above injustice which is not allowed elsewhere.—l remain yours, LIVE AND LET LIVE.

div.head: SHOCKING ACCIDENT DIMING POLITICAL REJOICINGS.
div.p: SHOCKING ACCIDENT DIMING POLITI- CAL REJOICINGS.

Late tin Tuesday night a man named William Litt, axed 46, was run over and I,illed in the main street of Keswick by a conveyance in which Mr. J. W. Lowther, M.P., his wife and children, were being drawn by a number of men aud boys. Mr. Lowthei arrived by the last train to take up his residence for a season on the shore of Derwentwater, and some of his ardent sup- porters, somewhat against his wish, unharnessed the horses from the landau and themselves dragged it. While the conveyance was going at a goed speed down- hill Litt ran across the street to get hold of the off Bide rope, but he fell, and the two wheels passed over his head, killing him almost immediately. Two ethers were also thrown down. One of them, Joseph Pearson, was taken to the hospital ; the third man was not seriously hurt. An inquest was held on Wednesday afternoon on the body of Litt, and a verdict of accident- ally killed was returned. The deceased leaves a widow and large family. Mr. and Mrs. Lowther, who were xreatly distressed by the accident, called upon the widow on Wednesday morning.

div.head: WESLEYAR CONFERENCE.
div.p: THE WESLEYAR CONFERENCE.

The Representative Session of the Wesleyan Confer- ence commenced on Monday. The President (Dr. Waller) in the course of his address referred to the political con- test in which many of them had recently taken part. There were, he said, members of different camps among them, and they were now • assembled, not as Conserva- tives or as Liberals, but as Methodists. 'Many important questions would come before them. One of these was the education question, on which he wished to remark, as he cid before the Royal Commission, that no addi- tional financial aid could be given either from the Con- solidated Fund or the rates which would be satisfactory Without adequate public representation. Other points enforced were the need for an increase in the number of local preachers and in the Income of the Home Mission- ary Fund. The glory of Methodism was, said Dr. Waller that the strong helped the weak. In the course of a short discussion on the endowments of Methodism, Dr. Henry Pope said the Board of Trustees for Chapel Pur- poses only possessed about £Bs,ooo—invested chietly for the enfranchisement of ground rents. The ministers bad no personal interest in the matter, and if the whole of the endowments in the Connexion ceaucl to-morrow not more than three ministers would be withdrawn. Their chapels, schools, and ministers' houses were of no possible use or advantage to Methodism without the loyal support ot the people year by year. Next year's Conference is to be held in Liverpool.

The Wesleyan Conference on Tuesday considered the question of itinerancy. The Rev. Fl. P. Hughes moved a resolution declaring the hearty adhesion of the Con- ference to the principle of itinerancy and tt4e three years' limit as a gencral rule,but acknowledging the desirable- ness of extension in certain cases,and appointing a com- mittee to consider the subject in its legal and other bearings, so that when it was submitted to the judg- ment of the members of the Connexion their response might be definite and decisive. Mr. Hughes said he would put the burden of proof in every case upon thole wanting exceptional treatment. Mr. J. Corry Monk- house seconded th. motion. Dr. Rigg said he thought three years was sufficient for a missionary, but in cir- cuits it was often desirable to extend the term for five years—no longer,—and he moved an amendment to Mr. Hughes' motion. Mr. John Cooper (Manchester) said he did not believe in tcuching tho 11th clause at all. Ul- timately Mr. Hughes' proposal was carried, with the ad- dition of the words moved by Mr. Cooper declaring that the Conference was not prepared to sanction the applica- tion to Parliament for the unconditional repeal of the 11th clause of the Deed Poll, or of that portion of it which limited successive appointments to three years.

At the Wesleyan Conference on Wednesday a Special Committee appointed last year presented a resolution in favour of" permitting the election of a woman repre- sentative to the Conference when in the judgment of any district synod such an election would serve the best in- terests of the work of God." The Rev. H. P. Hughes moved the acceptance of this resolution, and Mr. M. Atkinson (Leeds) seconded the motion. The Rev. Dr. Jenkins, in opposing it, said he had talked the matter over with Methodist women, who had invariably re- garded this proposal with nislike and distrust. The Rev. H. A. Scott moved "the previous question." The Itry. W. L. Watkinson said that throughout the world there was no instance of women in ecclesiastical assemblies. Some had said that women were unfit for the office; he would only say they were too good. The Rev. J. S. Simon supported the resolution. On a division "the previous question" was carried by 187 to 169, the Con- ference thus coming to no definite decision on the subject. At Thursday's sitting of the Wesleyan Conference the Secretary reported the stater:, the Connexion as follows: —Total number of members in Society, 437.722 ; teem- hers on trial, 30.050 ; junior members, 72,927; class leaders' ~ 26,100; local prchers, 17,095 ; net increase in Church membership. 4,372. The report on educational affairs stated that there were 788 day school depart- ments, a decrease of 23 on the year, and spoke of the difficulties imposed upon school managers by Die Government requirements with regard to premises and school plant. Dr. Rigg moved that the Conference should appiint a special comrmttee to consider the sub- ject of national education. Fie denied that he was pledged to the Archbilthrps' bill which was, he said, impracticable. Let th rn try to keep up their Wesleyan day schools. The resolution was agreed to, and a further resolution authorised the committee to co- operate with the representa'ives of other Nonconfcr-nist Churches. The Conference also passed a series of re- solutions calling for the establishment of School Boards everywhere, acting in districts of sufficient area.and the placing af a Christian unsectarian school within reason- able distance of every farnily,declaring that there ought to be no increased grant to denominational schools eithes from the local rates or from the Imperial taKes, unless such increased grgmt was accompanied by ade- quate and representative public management ; and urg- ing the importance of maintaining Wesleyan day scho)ls ira localities where it was found impossible to establish Fiction' Boards and Board anti,.ola of the kind in iicated.

-dew- Thomas Bond, 29, was c nvicred at the Stafford Assizes, on Monday, of murdeoing Frederick Bramwell, a small farmer, and George II ,ekett, Brkmwell's step- son, at Orgyeave, near Lichil•-1(1„ on the 31st May, and was senteneed to death. The prisoner was positively identified by Mrs. Bramwvll ac the man who committed the crime, and his presence in the immediate neighbour- hood at the time of the tragedy was proved by a large ouovvr of witieggeg. No motive for the act was shown.

It has hitherto been our custom to submit a list of the results of the respective examinations held in connec- tion with the classes conducted under the responsibility of the Technical Instruction Committee, but as a great many results are yet wanting to complete such a state- moot and an opportunity will, we believe, shortly pre- sent itself when the examination returns can be more fully dealt with,we wenture to omit them this year frnm our report.

As the statement of accounts (a copy of which has been sent to each member)es a true reflex of the year's , operations, which must of a necessity be largely con- trolled by the spending departments, we wilt venture to criticise the balance sheet for the best of all possible reasons, because our expenditure has exceeded our in- come. Commencing the year with a balance in hand of , £1 63. 411, we closed our books on the 30th June,show- ing an amount overdrawn to the extent of £ll 9s. 51d., in other words our income, including the balance, £1 63. 4e1., was £328 163. 7d., and our expenditure £340 6i. 00. It may prove interesting to the majority of you it we briefly serrate the causes contributing to this adverse balance, so that you may be in a better position to judge whether our stewardship meets with your ap- probation or otherwise. Adverting to the Park account you will find the receipts from visitor's fees, and park tickets were £3l Os. Sd.,a slight increase over last year, and a decrease of £7, when compared with 1893. The bowling greens have produced £2O 93. 141. against £25 193. li3. in 1891, a decrease of £5 Bs. 33.,which is owing to number 1 green having to be closed the greater part of this season con- sequent upon a portion of it being relaid. With dimin- ishing receipts in this account, we have unfortunately had increasing expenses, sods and bone dust alone cost- ing £l6 93.101 which is an additional item this year. Before leaving the park account, you will observe, by a glance at the balance sheet, that the suggestion thrown out at the last annual general meeting relative to prizes being offered to the bowlers has been put into opera- tion. At the first meeting of the committee it was un- animously agreed that £2 be set apart to provide prizes for a bowling handicap. This £2 together with the entrance fees £1 23.. placed to £3 23. at the disposal of the sub-committee chosen to carry out the handicap,and they divided it into six prizes and awarded them as follows :-Ist prize, £1 53., 2nd prize, 153., E. Scott and ' W. Hemmings tied, the first and second prizes were therefore equally divided between them ; 3rd prize, Ss. 6d., J. T. Thompson ; 4th prize, 63., R. Sherlock ; ' sth prize. 3s. 63., H. Stanton ; 6th prize, 33., T. Compton. In addi'ion to the £2 voted to the bowlers, the committee considered it only ,fair that the playing members of the cricket club should have some further inducement to excel, and conquently placed a similar amount at the disposal of the Cricket Club Com- mittee to be given in privs in such a manner as they deemed best in the interests of the club. The £2 was awarded in equal proportions to, and received by Messrs. R. Bell, G. Husband, W. H. Crowther and T. Clare, Jun. Although the total revenue on the general account is £6 less than in 1894, the expenses show a very material reduction, which we venture to think renders explana- tioe superfluous. The Library is perhaps more than any other account responsible for the overdraft. A cursory survey reveals the fact that £9B 143. 23. was expended, as against £62 17s. 11d, last year. an increase of £36. This heavy expenditure is really due, as no doubt you are all aware, to preparing, printing, and binding the new catalogue. As to the necessity for such an outlay, the reasons are obvious and were dealt with at length in our last annual report. For fear that some of the members might think the price charged for the catalogue, viz., four- pence each, is too much, we beg to say that the east of preparing and printing works out at Is. 21d. each, or a net loss on each copy at mid. and less ethers should say it could have been done cheaper, we also assure them that one of the tenders for printing and binding, is apart from the cost of prepara- tion, averaged is. Sid each, or a penny more than it actually cost to place it in your hands in its present complete state. That such a record of the books in the Library has been a boon to the members, is evident from the fact that in 1893, we had 220 readers, and an issue covering 12 months,of 5878 books,whereas we have now 333 readers, an increase of over 50 per cent. The issues for the 32 weeks, i.e. from the 12th November when the Library was re-opened, to the 30th June, were 6469, re- presenting an increase of 78 per cent. We feel warranted in stating that never since the Library was formed,haa it it been in such a healthy condition ; not only as to the number of hooks issued, which you will readily perceive is equal to 100 volumes per night, but as to the class of books it contains,for the shelves are stored with volumes representing what is best in literature on almost very eubject. May the best use of this Library be to strengthen good resolutions in the yoking, in the direc- tion of manfulness arid self-help ; may it teach the salu- tary lesson how to enjoy a little thankfullv,and to endure much bravely, leading to the habit of mind which has no sympathy with frivolity, irreverence or debasing views of life. May the use of it implant in the Minna of many a love of literature and science which will beautify their daily existence, and render it happier and more bearable, is the earnest wish of the President and your Committee." The Chairman said be thought they would all agree with him that the report which they had just heard read was a remarkably good one, not only for being ex- ' plieit in every way, but for the way it had been put together. He was sure every credit was due to the ' secri'ary for it. He was glad to hear there was a very large Increase in the number of those who took books out of the library. It showed that the men and boys were beginning to appreciate the library more than they had done before, and he was quite sure with regard to the catalogue there was not a better in existence ; it stood Al. He had heard it remarked that it was one of the most explicit catalme,ues in any circulating library in the country, and very great credit was due to the committee and the secretary for the way it had been got out. (Hear, hear.) With regard to the Sir Richard Moon scholarship, he had something to do with getting that increased Mr. Webb epeke to him about it, and it was thought that the RUM of £4O would not keep a lad either in college or school, and in order to make it better it was now, as they had heard. £BO, but in place of the competition being yearly, it was every alternate year. That would enable a ynung fellow to keep himself whilst he was at college, and he hoped some of the students would bestir themselves in future, and not let these rich plums go to Wolverton or Crewe ; let them have one or two in that department, and he hoped they would try and do their , beet in that respect. (Applause.) The report and balance sheet were afterwards adopted. Mr. Gilmour said it had been considered year after year what improvements could be made in connection , with the Institute, and he referred to the good which had been derived from the Viaduct Institute in Technical education.

div.head: GOOD TEMPLARY.
div.p: GOOD TEMPLARY.

The weekly session of the Hope of Earlestown Lodge of Good Templars was held at the Co-opera- tive Hall,on Monday evening. Bro. Wilson presided, and there was a fair attendance of members. Bro. Q.M. Sergeant Roberts, and Bro. Ashley of the Pres- cot Lodge was present as visitors. A letter was read from s member of the" Gleam and Sunshine" lodge,Tranmere, expressing thanks for the recent visit which the Earlestown lodge paid them, and for the encouraging character of the entertainment, and hoping to return the visit shortly. Messrs. Wilson, Clarke,Newman and Barker,were appointed a committee to draw up the programme for the en- siling quarter. The officers for the next quarter were elected and will be installed at the next meet- ing. The programme for the evening was " short readings." Interesting items were read by Bros. Newman, Hatton, Dale, and Clarke, and Bro. War- burton gave a recitation. Encouraging addresses were given by Bros. Roberts and Ashley.
POLICE AUGMENTATION.

The police force of Earlestown has been further increased by the transfer from Nelson of P.C. Tivney. Although much needed, it is not expected that any further augmentation will take place at present. RUNAWAY HORSES AT EARtusTowlsr.

About four o'clock on Wednesday afternoon, a carter in the employ of the Midland Railway Co, left his two horses and dray, en the Railway Bridge in front of Messrs. T. and T. Vicar's works, whilst he went into the office to obtain a signature in his delivery book. Whilst he was away a train passing under the bridge startled the horses and-they set off down the incline towards Earle-street, at a mad pace. At the bottom they turned the corner sharply and when opposite the shop of Mr. Siddeley, which almost faces the road to the bridge, the leading chain horse fell on the curbstone and the shaft horse falling over it, came in contact with a corner of the window, smashing the framework and glass to fragments. Several children were abJut, but Mr. Chorlton seeing the danger hurried them into his shop for safely. Beyond a slight scratch which the chain horse received, the animals were not injured, and were able to continue their journey to Warrington.

div.head: 1.0b.T.-EARLESTOWN EBENEZER LODGE.
div.p: 1.0b.T.-EARLESTOWN EBENEZER LODGE.

This lodge held its weekly session in the Co-op- erative Hall, on Tuesday night. Bro. Taylor read the quarterly circular, after which the election of officers for the ensuing quarter was proceeded with, the following being elected :—C.T., Bro. W.Hatton ; V.T., Sister Hatton; sec., Bro. T. Dean; fin. sec., Bro. H. Brown ; treas., A. Morris ; chaplain, Sister Brown; mar., Bro. W. Strong; guard, Bro. Fish ; sentinel, Bro. Williams. Two members were ini- tiated, and Sister Ward,from Wolverhampton, made a few remarks on the progrPss of the Order there. Bro. J. Taylor gave a song, and Bro. Morris a recita- tion, after which the lodge was closed in due form by Bro. W. Hatton. NEWTON-LE-WILLOWS HORTI CULTURAL SOCIETY. From an advertisement it will he seen that the annual exhibition of flowers, fruit, &c ,will be held on Saturdsy afternoon on the ground of the Earles- town Football Club. This year the committee have made a new venture, by introducing athletic sports The prizes for bicycle and foot races have been on view during the week, and are of a first-class des- cription,embracing marble clocks,Vienna regulators, &c. There have been a large number of entries, in- cluding a good number from Warrington, and,given fine weather, the affair should be a decided success.

EARLICSTOWN MISSION SUNDAY SCHOOL. On Thursday afternoon the children attending the Sunday school attached to the Earlestown Mission were entertained to tea in the Co-operative Hall. The children, who are drawn from the poorer classes, to the number of about 90,assembled at the Hall about two o'clock, and after romping for an hour or two, sat down to a substantial tea, their wants being attended to by nr. and Mrs. Drinq, assisted by a number of volunteer workers. After tea the children were taken to Mr. Sanderson's field, where they enjoyed themselves until dusk, and dispersed thoroughly pleased with their enter- tainment. BURTONWOOD SCHOOL BOARD.

The usual monthly ineeting of the above Board was held in the class-room of the Board Schools, Burtonwood, on Tuesday, when there were present, Messrs. James Warburton (chairman), Andrew Jackson (vice-chairman), William Fairclough, Thomas Norcott and Rev. A. M. Mitchell ; 11. Gaw- thorps (4chool master), and William Webster (clerk). The correspondence of the month was considered. The report of the drawing examination which was " Good " was read. The Clerk reported the schools had been used by both political parties for meetings and by the Returning officer for a polling station during the late Parliamentary elec- tion. The treasurer's book showing receipt of £72 193 amount of rate lie. 74., books sold and 53: hire of schools, since last meeting. SONS OF TEMPER A.NCE.

The usual meeting the Samuel Morley Section of Cadets was held in the Co-opera- tive Hall. Rev. J. Judson presided. After the opening ceremony Bro. W. Wheittly entertained the juveniles with a description of his visit to London. Fie referred to the kindnevs of the Rev. Thomas Wynne Jones,formerly of Fltrlestown, who had pro- vided homes for the party and met them on the steps of St. Paul's Cathedral and conducted them round the City for several days. He described the visits to St. Pauls, Wesminster Abbey, the Houses of Parliament, Hyde Park, and gave a very vivid description of the glitter and attractiveness of the London gin palaces. The adult society met at 8 o'clock. Bro. J. Pickett presided. After the open- ing, the annual report of National Division held in Glasgow in Whitweek was presented and extracts were given with explanations by Bro. W. Pearson, and J. Judson. One special feature was that there had been only six days' si,!kne+4 per 1.000 member for the year; also six deaths per 1,000 member for the same time.

div.head: DEATH OF MIL THOM.A.S CROSBY, OF RUNCORN
div.p: DEATH OF MIL THOM.A.S CROSBY, OF RUNCORN
THE FUNERAL.

Many will hear with regret of the death of Mr. Thomas Crosby, who resided in Greenway-road, Runcorn, and carried on the business of a boot and shoe dealer in Regent-street. About five weeks ago he had an attack of pneumonia and pleurisy. He was attended by Dr. Brunton, locum tent-its for Dr. McDougall, aril seemed to be making satisfactory progress towards recovery. But on Saturday and Sunday Dr. McDougall and Dr. Brunton had their anxiety aroused through his weakness of heart, and on Monday morning at 2.30 he passed peacefully away through failure of the heart's action. Mr. Crosby who was well known in Runcorn and district was a member of St. Paul's Wesleyan Chapel, and proved himself most useful in the work of the church in many ways. He associated himself with the Liberal cause, and was a member of the Liberal execu- tive committee. On Wednesday last, feeling much better, he went to record his vote for Sir John T. Brunner, Bart. lie leaves a widow, one son, and three daughters to mourn his loss. The funeral took place at Runcorn Cemetery on Thursday afternoon. A number of local gentlemen formel in procession at the house and walked to the cemetery as a imrk of respect. At the head there walked the Revs. W. George and J. ' H. Tite, and Dr. McDougall, followed by Messrs. H. Darling,ton,T Leach,Jas. Knowles,T.Simister,F.L. Scott, S.Coventry,P.T. Lawton,J.W. Woodland,Ja roes Gregory, R. Morris, John Leathwood, W. Ackerley, J. Mackinson, John Coxhill, °Diver, A. Unsvvorth. Jones, T. Cooke, P. Brown, J. Dowdle, William Handley, A. R. Norman and E. Marshall. Owing to the short distance to be traversed to the Cemetery the coffin was placed on a bier and borne on the shoulders of the following hearers: Messrs. W. Roach, W. Page, W. Brimelow, T. Dean, J. Leadstone, J. Stanway, and C. Kniveton. The coffin was of oak with brass mountings. There were no flowers, by request. Immediately behind the coffin, there walked Mr. B. Crnsby (son.). Rev. C- E. Norman (soc -in-law), Messrs. Crosswaite, Peacocke, T. Cooke, B. Kiveton, J. Berkett, T. Carr, Darlington, Stone, Joseph 13, zt• r D. H. Jones, C. Mainwaring, Albert Smith, Ephraim eoltsworth and F. ELECTION OF COMMITTEE.

The Chairman then declared the result of the ballot for the election of six members of the Committee to he as follows :—Messrs. C. W. Emmett, J. R. Allan, P. Connor, J. Andertnn.J. Barcroft,and W. Davies. Messrs. W. Sephton and FL Ff. Anderton were appointed audi- torl, and Messrs. J. Gee and W. Clare, jun., scruitneers. Mr. D. Garnett,said it appeared it had been arranged to give three lectures during th I coming winter, and he asked if they coold not give a concert, and science lec- ture also.

The Chairman said the lectures had to bs arranged for early in the year, as unless that was done they could not get held of the best men, and that was the reason why the Committee had selected the lectures referred to as they thought they were good men. No doubt a con- cert would be interspersed with the lectures. He hoped to get some gentleman to distribute the prizes, either jest before Christmas or a little after, and that would give ono concert and a little amusement after. (Hear, hear.)

Mr. Gilmour raised a question as to the voting, and I said it was not fair that the men should vote for one or I two candidates only, when six were required. The Chairman was glad Mr. Gilmour had mentioned the matter. He said 35 had voted for one candidate. A- Mr. Gilmour said,thev wanted six members and they might as well have voted for the lot as one : 48 voted for two 111 voted for 3 ; 147 voted 4 ; 113 voted for 5 ; and 579 voted for 6, so that they would see that only 579, or about one half of the members only voted for as many members as were wanted, and he hoped they would all vote for the number required. Mr. Graham moved a vote of thanks to the Chairman and Mr. W. Clare secooded.—Mr. Ormand said the com- mittee and members were very much indebted to the President for that room being beautified in the manner it had been. It had been done without any cost to the members, and he thought it was as little as they could do to propose a vote of thanks to him. Since the last meeting, Mr. Emmett had seen added to the bench of magistrates. They knew what Mr. Emmett had been in the past, and that gave them every faith and confi- dence as to the future, so that if it was their misfortune to go before him they knew he would temper justice with mercy. (Applause and laughter.)—The vote was unanimously accorded, and the Chairman having briefly acknowledged, the meeting was brought to a close.

div.head: NORTHUMBERLAND MINERS AND THE TRADES UNION CONGRESS.
div.p: NORTHUMBERLAND MINERS AND THE TRADES UNION CONGRESS.

DECISION TO WITHDRAW. The result of the vote of the miners of Northumber- land on the question of whether or not they are to be re- presented at the forthcoming meeting of the Trades' Union Congress,which is to be held at Cardiff in Septem- ber next, has now been completed. In sending out the voting papera,the members of the Executive Committee stated that the Durham miners had already determined not to be represented at the Congress, and they also were unanimously of opinion that the meeting was now nothing more than a Socialist assemblage, and they I therefore recommended that no representative be sent. The men have taken the same view, for in spite of the fact that some of the miners urged that it would be better to attend the Cougrese, in order to counteract the Socialist leanings, only three or four colliers have voted in favour of representation, the final result of the vote being that, like the miners of the neighbouring county, the Northumberland men have decided by a large • majority to take no further pail in the Congress.

WARRINGTON. SUDDEN DEATH AT CROFT.

On Saturday evening a painful sensation was caused in the village ot Croft by the sudden death death of Miss Charnock, of Swithy-brow, Croft, a maiden lady 72 years of age. The deceased had been in her garden, and bad spoken to several persona who were passing, and appeared in good spirits. A short time alter entering the house she sat down to supper,of which she partook heartily, but imme- diately after complained of feeling very ill, and expired in about five minutes. Death is due to heart disease.

THE WARRINGTON EMULATOR OF "TOMMY BURNS." Robinson who attempted to walk 100 miles in 24 consecutive hours, at the same time pushing a wheelbarrow, has failed. He has succeeded in walk- ing from the Marquis of Granby to Liverpool and back in less than 8 hours, and having had a wash and a rub down, he started for Manchester. On reaching Patricroft Robinson was seized with a severe attack of cramp, and though efforts were made by his attendants to restore him they were unsuccessful, and the task bad accordingly to be abandoned. Robinson has not, however, despaired of success, and it is freely stated that he will at no very distant date make another attempt. HOUSEHOLD LINENS, hemmed and marked free of charge.— J. and W. Dutton, Sankey-et.. Warrington.—Adnt. WORKINGMEN'S GOSPEL TEMPERANCE MISSION.

The usual open-air meeting under the auspices of this mission was held on Saturday evening, Mr. J. Drury and Mrs. Owen, of Penketh, conducting the proceedings. In his address Mr. Drury said that if workingnaen would spend their wages in food and clothing for themselves, their wives' and their children, instead of spending it with the wealthy publican, very much less talk would be heard about low wages, bad trade, and poverty. Neither Liberalism,T)ryism' " Socialism," "Labour- ism," nor any other ism would keep them godly and sober. This could only be effected by Christianity and total abstinence.—On Sunday night another open-air meeting was held by the mission,when the evils of intemperance were pointed out, and the blessings yf teetotalism commented upon,.

The monthly meeting of the above was held on Tuesday at the Blue Lion Hotel,ldarket-place,there being a good attendance of delegates. After the routine business, circulars were read from the London Trades Council taking exception to the new standing orders of the Parliamentary Com- mittee of the Trades Union Congress debarring Trades Councils being represented at future Con- gresses, and urging the Council to endorse the action of the London Trades Council in sending delegates to the Congress to be held in Cardiff in September next, and insisting upon the rights of Trades Councils to be represented, a re- presentation to which they have been entitled from the very inception of Trades Congresses. The Warrington Trades Council not being in a position to send &legates, endorsed the action of the Lon- don Trades Council in the endeavour to maintain the right they have enjoyed so long. A boy, named Mark Rose, 11 years of age, who resides with his parents at Stone Croft, Runcorn, received most peculiar treatment at the hands of a number of his fellows on Sunday It appears that a number of boys whose ages ranged from 11 to 17 years, proceeded to Higher Runcorn on Sunday evening. Rose was in company with them, and against him the other boys seem to have had some antipathy. At any rate they fastened him to a gate, and afterwards stripped him of his clothing, and then, it is alleged,. rolled him down a railway embankment. He was also beaten, and then left to his fate. His screams were heard by Mr. Ackerley, a farmer, of Higher Runcorn, and on going to Rose he 1 ound him in an unconscious condition. Ile was carried to the house of Mr. Copper where he recovered consciousness. Subsequently he was taken home, and is now recovering from the shock he received.

div.head: WA mtISGTON CLERGY INSTITUnONS.
div.p: THE WA mtISGTON CLERGY INSTITUnONS.
ANNIVERSARY MEETING.

The anniversary of the Warrington Institutions for Clergy Widows and Orphans, and Clergy Daughters' School, was kept at Warrington on Thursday, The pro- ceedings of the day commenced with a meeting of sub- scribers, -77hich was held in the Training Coiledle, com- mencing at 11.15, when the minutes and reports were and confirmed, grants approved, and members appointed on the Committee of Management. At the conclusion of this meeting divine service was held in the Parish Church, at 12.15, when a sermon was preached by the Yen. Archdeacon of MacclesflAd. This was followed by a dinner in the Clergy Daughters' School, when approp- riate toasts were submitted and suitably responded to.

Mr. RALPH BROCICLEBANIC presided over the meeting of subscribers and there were alao present, amongst others the Dean of Manchester, the Archdeacon of Chester, the Archdeacon of Macclesfield, Archdeacon Gore (Bowdon), the Rev. Canon Maitland Wood (vicar of Runcorn), the Rev. Canon Penrhyn (rector of Winwick),the Rev. Canon Willis (rector of Warrington); the Rev. Canen Black- burne, the Rev. E. C. E. Carleton, the Rev. Mr. Holmes, and Mr. Henry Greenall (treasurer). CLERGY WIDOWS AND ORPHANS PENSION FUND.

The Rev. Canon PENRHYN. rector of Winwick (hon. secretary of the Clergy Widows and Orphan' Pension Fund), read the following report :--Your committee in once more presenting their annual report have again to deplore the death of several valued friends and sup- porters. Nearly a year has elapsed since Canon Heron, who had for very many years proved himself a most useful member of committee, was called to his rest, and in the be4inning of this year we were deprived of the help so ungrudgingly given to us by Canon Heywood, and a lay member of our committee, Mr. W. Fox, has since been taken from us. Mrs. Fraser, too, the widow of the late Bishop of Manchester,who was a warm friend of our institutions, has very lately passed away,and has bequeathed to us a very generous donation. Your com- mittee would suggest that that the vacancies thus caused should be filled up by the appointment of the following : Rev. H. B. Blogg, of Frodsham, v. Canon Heron ; Rev. Hon. A. Lyttelton v. Canon Heywood, and Mr. R. Brocklebank v. Mr. W. Fox. Mr. J. Charlton Parr having on the ground of I ill-health declined to fill the place of the late Sir Gilbert Greenall, the name of Mr. James Tinsley is submitted for your approval. Norther names having been sent in to the Secretary, the retiring members have been re-elected, subject to their confirma- tion by the subscribers at the annual meeting :—Chester, the Rev. Richard Greenall, Canon Blencowe, and Messrs. James Tinsley and J. H. Grafton ; Manchester, the Rev. Canon Birley and the Rev. Hon. A. Lyttelton, and Messrs. W. P. Fullagar and H. W. Worsley Taylor ; Liverpool, the Rev. Hon. Canon Bridgman and the Rev. Canon Blundell, and Mr. R. Ireland Blackburne and the Right Hon. the Earl of Lathom. One grant left last year for further inquiries by the Secretary was subsequently paid, bringing up the total to £2,135, and four small grants amounting to £25 have been made in cases of special need 'on the responsibility of the Treasurer and Secretary. Of those aided last year four Manchester widows have died and one has re-married, and one Chester widow has withdrawn her application. There are, on the other hand, fresh applications from five widows in Manchester Diocese, one widow in Chester and one in Liverpool Diocese, but there are no fresh orphans' applications. The annual meeting are asked to sanction pensions, donations, and payments for free scholars at the Clergy Daughters' School to the amount of £2,155, and if the recommendations of your committee are approved, there will be on our list from Chester 19 widows and ten orphans, Liverpool twelve widows and ten orphans, and from Manchester 31 widows, 23 orphans, and free edu- cation for six orphans, one from Chester, two from Liverpool, and three from Manchester. The income of tho charity for the year ended December 31st, 1894, was £2.161 Bs., made up as follows :—Special donations, £lOl 93. 61. ; interest in capital, £719 Ils. 51. ; collec- tions. £467 12s. 51.; subscriptions, £748 133. 3d., un- appropriated fund, Chester and Liverpool, £llO 23. id.; and bank interest. £13193. 41 ; as arrainsttbe following figures respectively in 1893 t £36 103., £719 75., £504 23. 11d., £733 193. 101., £ll2 103., and £5 63. Id. This shows a slight increase in subscriptions, but a decrease in church collections, and it Is hoped that in the present year both items may snow an increase, and we may have such an income at our disposal as may enable us to deal liberally with those who are new applicants, as well as somewhat to augment the very morkra.te grants which have been made to the applicants of former years. CLERGY DAUGHTERS' SCHOOL.—TH'E ALLEGED UNFIEALTHINERS OF WARRINGTON.

The lies,. Canon Vitztus (hon. secretary of the above school) presented the following report :—My Lords and gentlemen,—The past year has been one of trial and anxiety to this institution. Ever since last August the great question under continual consideration has been the removal of the school, and the uncertainty arising therefrom has disturbed the usual quiet routine and doubtless affected the numbers. Various causes have contributed to create a feeling in favour of change on the part of some of the parents, teachers, and commit- tee. Supposed unhealthiness, smells from the river, smoke from the manufactories, and the scarcity of country walks have been the chief. Of these, the first has been proved to be purely imaginary ; the second, there is a strong reason to believe, was but temporary ; the last two it is true exist. All these causes have pos- sibly lowered the numbers, and produced a desire for change, but there may be other reasons, just as real,for the present decrease, notably the reduced incomes of the clergy, making even the small charge of £25 per head a great consideration, and the up-growth of high schools in nearer localities. The committee have given the matter their most careful consideration, and in the face of the great uncertainty at present as to the real cause of the fall, the serious difficulties attendant upon a removal of the school, and the manifest advan- tages of the present situation, which more than counter- balance many of the disadvantages, have come to the conclusion not to take any further steps at present, hut wait until it is perfectly clrar that it is wise and right to move or alter in any way the constitution of the school. In the meantime it is satisfalory to know from the doctor and the headmistress that the physical and moral condition of the scholars is all that could be desired, and from the examiner that their intellectual and spiritual Progress are satisfactory. These reports I can fully en- dorse. During the winter term the Bible classes were held in three divisions. chapters from the books of Levi- tieus, Numbers and Deuteronomy being read. In the spring the gospels for the Sunday were studied, the girls being divided into two sections, older and younger. During tie latter part of the summer term we have been taking a general survey of the books from which the lessons for the day are chosen, namely, Ezra, Esther and Nehemiah, with the corresponding prophecies of Haggai and ZAchariah, and the hook of Job. The services have been held as usual throughout the year, those at the chapel being, WA believe, a delight as well as a help to all who take part in them. A very enjoy- able re-union of past and Present pupils took place on the 10th July. The proceedings t•egan with a special service in the chapel, most beautifully rendered by the girls. This was followed by luncheon, tennis, supper and dancing, and after an early celebration of the Holy Communion the next morning the party broke up. I believe these well attended gatherings not only give the greatest pleasure,but witness in the best way possble to the interest and affection that is felt in and for the school by its former pupils. MISS BEAL'S REPORT.

The report of MiSS MART J. BEAL, head mistress, was read as follows :—I have much pleasure in presenting to you my report of the schonl during the term which ended on the 25th•inet. The health of the girls has been very good, with the exception of seven Cas,'S of mumps to- wards the close of the term. The conduct has been ex- cellent. There am M girls in the school-15 Chester : Two orphans, one Ps.. on. S.T. ;14 Liverpool: Four orphans, two P.S. ; 18 Manchester : Eleven orphans, three P.S., one ST. ; seven extra diocesan : One orphan. The conduct of the girls holding the various exhibitions bas been excellent. There are two vacant exhibitions, one school and one "First year,"as two exhibitioners are leaving. Forty girls entered for the Itoval Drawing Society examination, 23 obtained pass, and eight hon- ours certificates. Two girls obtained full certificates, having obtained honours in all six divisions. Three girls RPM highly commended for drawings sent to the annual exhibition of the same society. Some girls entered for the Cambridge higher local examination, held in Jose. The results are not yet published. The nom tined Oxford local and school examination was held at the school dur- ing the week beginning July 15th. The results of the local examinations will not be nut till the end of August or later. The Rev. J. Worsley Cundey was the school examiner. Reports as to the result of examinations were also read from the Rev. J. Worsley Cundey, and A. C. Clapin, M.A. The DEAN of MANCHESTER said he wished to refer to the report of the Rector of Warrington on the clergy Daughters' School. Some of the language of the report did not appear to him to be entirely judicial. There was no doubt that the question of the removal should be carefully considered, and also impartially. There was a great deal to be said in favour of the removal of the school, although the statement of difficulties seemed to him to have been overput. He contended that the ' question had been prejudiced by the introduction of certain adjectives and expletives which appeared to be a little out of place on that occasion. It was not a sun- position for there were manufactories in Warrington. He supposed that the people of Warrington rejoiced in them. He for one was determined to do all he could to prevent the school going down. There were other interests besides those to which reference had been made which he, as a churchman, held to be equally dear. He would not introduce them at that meeting, nor would he oppose the passing of the report, although he regretted he was unable to attend the meeting of the committee which was held on the previous day, when it was submitted. He honed the qaestion woull be carefully considered before it was too late. lArchdeacon GORE said that notwithstandingthe 5m.119 the school had flourished until quite recently. div.head: WALKING DAY AT STRETTON.
div.p: WALKING DAY AT STRETTON.

The annual Walking Day at Siretton took place on Friday week. About 200 children and old scholars assembled in church at 130, and after a short service they all adjourned to the Vicarage gardens, where they were regaled with buns and ginger wine. They then marched round the village, headed by the band of the Blue Coat School, meet- ing afterwards in the Vicarage field for games and sports. At five o'clock an excellent tea was pro- vided in the schools, the caterers being Mr. and Mrs. Howard who gave every satisfaction. Num- bers of the parishioners joined the party after tea, and the weather being propitious a very enjoyable evening was spent. At a ball, subsequently given in the schoolroom, about 150 were present, and dancing was kept up till 12.30. On Sunday the school sermons were preached, that in the morning by the Vicar, and that in the evening by the Rev. L. B. Radford, M.A., second master of the Grammar School, Warrington. The offertolies amounted to £l5, which with £4l 108, sul>criptions, makes £56 103. given by the parishioners towards the maintenance of their schools.

CHURCH SUNDAY SCHOOL TEACHERS. MEETING.

A meeting for recreation of the 'members of the Warrington and District Sunday School Teachers' Association was held at the Rectory, on Saturday afternoon, when about 120 ladies and gentlemen assembles. Games were indulged in until five o'clock, when an excellent tea was served in the , Fairfield Schools. After the tea, which was thoroughly enjoyed, the party re-assembled at the Rectory.when games, &c.,were again resumed until eight o'clock. Then all attended a special service in the Parish Church, where an interesting address was given by the Rev. E. Elma Harding, principal of St. Aidan s Theological College, Birkenhead, who took for his text the words, "So when they had dined Jesus saith to Simon Peter, Simon, son of Jonas, !avast thou Me more than these ? He saith unto Him : Yea, Lord, Thou knowest that I love Thee. He Faith unto him : Feed my Lambs" (St. John xxi. 15). At the termination of the service the patLy dispersed to their respective homes. In the evening from six o'clock until eight o'clock, the Blue Coat School brass hand was in attendance,and played an excellent selection of music, tHE ARRANGEMENTS FOR AUGUST AT THE PARK. _ _

RUNCOLN URBAN DISTRICT COUNCIL.

A meeting of this Council was held in Runcern Town Hall, on Thursday morning. Mr. J.W. Lightburn occu- pied the chair and there were also present—Revs. Dr. Gaetald' Messrs. P. Speakman, J.P., C.C. S. Taylor, J.P. CC., F. Wiswall, D. Biabrown M. C.C., J. Jones, H. J. Grice W. Collier, J. Wilson, T. Dean, G. Hewitt, and Mr. F. A. Lake (law clerk), Mr. Marshail (secretary), Dr. McDougall (medical officer) and Mr. M. Barker (surveyor).
MEDICAL OFFICER'S REPORT.

The report of Dr. McDougall -(m-e-diCli.officer) stated that the number of deaths registered during the past month amounted to 65. Two were inquest cases, and of the remaining 63, 28 were due to measles, 4to bron- chitis, 3te convulsions, 6 to diarrhcea, 7 to mesenteric disease. 2 to congestion of the lungs, 2 to diphtheria, 2 to scarlatina, and one each to paralysis, tubercular disease, heart disease, enteric fever, anaemia, phthisis, cancer, dropsy, and pneumonia. The above 65 deaths showed an average death rate of 41 per thousand of the estimated population and exclusive of the inquest cases of 397. Forty-three births were registered during the month.—Dr. Gastaldi asked whether there was any cause visible to the Medical Officer for the case of enteric tever.—Dr. McDougall said it had been suggested that there was a cause and it was considered by the authority twelve months ago.
HIGHWAYS AND BUILDINGS COMMUTER.

This committee recommended that the tender of Mr T. Bradshaw for the alteration of machine house pre' mises and erection of boundary wall in respect of Low land-road improvement be accepted,and that the tender of Messrs.Billington and Boyle for the construction of a water closet and alteration of boundary wall in St. John- at. in respect of the improvement of such street be acceptod.—These minutes were passed on the motion of Mr. Taylor, seconded by Mr. P. Speakman.
HELLTIT COMMITTEE.

It was recommended— ii3?--ible--cOmmittee that the tenderof Messrs. Unsworth Bros. to supply the Sanitary Inspector's uniform clothing consisting of one overcoat, one coat, two pairs of trousers, one vest and one cap for the sum of seven guineas be accepted.—The minutes were passed without comment.

FINANCE. The reports of the Finance Committee were approved and adopted, and also the recommendation that the offer of Mrs. Elizabeth Meadowcruft to lend the sum of £l,OOO for five years at 3± per cent, interest per annum, payable half-yearly, be accepted (to pay off existing loan at .31 per cent. interest).

SIR JOHN T. BRUNNER, M.P., AND THE TRADES' HALL. The Secretary read a letter from Sir John T. Brunner, in which he said : I am very much gratified by the very kind appreciation shown by your Council of my gift of the Guild Hall. It was my pleasure yesterday to attend the first meeting of the Management Committee, as one of the representatives of your Council, and am glad to inform you that under the thoroughly business-like pre- sidency of your chairman, Mr. Imison, the Management Committee promises well to be economical and thorough. I share to the full the hope of the Council that the build- ing may be an advantage to the Societies which will assemble under its roof.
THE VOTE Or CONGRATULATION.

The following letter was also read from Sir John Brunner, M.P., with regard to the resolution of congrat- ulation which was passed at the last meeting of the Council :—" Winnington Old Hall, Northwich, Bth July, 1895. Dear Mr. Lake,—Pleatie convey to your Council on my behalf and on behalf of my wife, our cordial thanks for the very kind feeling shown in the unanimous passing of the resolution of congratulation to us. It has given me intense pleasure to read the public accounts of the speeches made on the occasion of the passing of this resolution.—Your faithfully, JogN T. BRuNxER."

div.head: SHIP OWNEiS AND TOLLS.
div.p: SHIP OWNEiS AND TOLLS.

The Law Clerk stated that he had received a letter from the Ship Owners' Association with reference to toll being charged for some vessels coming up to Runcorn by the Ship Canal, but going free to Manchester. The letter referred to certain complaints and the Association desired to submit them to the Council. He suggested that it would be well to refer the communication to the General Purposes Committee.—This was done on the motion of the Chairman, seconded by Dr. Gastaldi.

DR. GASTALDI AND TEED RAILWAY COMPANY. In accordance with notice given, Dr. Gaetaldi moved the following resolution :—" That a memorial from this Council be sent to the directors of the London and North-Western Railway Company urging the desirability in the interest of the said company, the travelling pub- lic and above all of the working classes, of a reduction in the existing transit per the footbridge and ferry ; to issue tickets available either for bridge or ferry ; and further to reduce the railway fares between Runcorn, Ditton, and Widnes."—He said one of the greatest re- cords In the history of Runcorn has been the completion and opening of the Runcorn Bridge which bad put the two towns of Widnes and Runcorn into more direct communication. Previously the people had no other means of approaching either of the places than by ferry. In 1868 the completion of the bridge opened anew era in the hist)ry of Runcorn. They should pay a tribute to Mr. Cunningham who earnestly worked to obtain a footpath on the bridge. He went to Londen and persuaded the committee to make the convenience for pedestrians to cross the structure. During the 27 years it had been opened, there had been constant transit to and fro. The receipts must have already paid for the cost of construc- tion. They bad no right to examine the books of the Railway Company,but they might by calculation estim- ate pretty accurately what they had received. If the receipts per diem reached £6O they found that in 27 years the income was £591.300 which was more than the cost of the structure. On looking into the history of the bridge fares they found that each passenger by rail paid 9d. to go to Ditton or Widnes from Runcorn, but this had been reduced to ed. each way. But the price originally fixed for foot passengers was maintained,viz., is. per week for season tickets. This was a great bur- den to working people. On May 10th,1884,a memorial was sent by the Commissioners to the directors of the railway company praying for a reduction of fares,it be- ing considered that 2e.i. single and 3d. return, and is. per week contract, was excessive. They asked for a re- duction to the extent of 1d: each way and ed. per con- tract, but nothing came of the effort. On May 9t13,1889, a similar petition was again made, supplemented by the signature of over 500 perse ns, who asked for the reduc- tion of the affairs to and from Liverpool, and for a pro- vision of a better service of trains between Runcorn, Warrington, and Manchester. Nothing, however, was done, although every chairman of the Commissioners in town had approached the subject. He believed there was no other bridge in the United Kingdom where 2d. was charged for pedestrians, and 6d. by rail. Formerly the tickets for the ferry or bridge could be used for either of the means of communication but that advantage had been taken away. He believed there was a watch being kept as to the number of per- sons utilising the ferry so that the small number could be used as an argument for its abandonment. He asked that residents should use it more frequently. He thought the Company should make improvements in the way of approaches for carts and carriages. He asked every member to support the motion. If the Company refused to hear them, it would be their duty to agitate in the counties of Lancashire and Cheshire for a vehicular bridge to be owned by the public.—Mr. Bisbrown in seconding the motion, said he agreed with the remarks made. The payment of tolls was against the spirit of the age, the great tendency being to reduce them to a very low figure or abolish them.—The Chairman thought they were beginning at the wrong end. They required to make out a case against the Railway Company. It was desirable to present a memorial in the best possible form, and any new element or fresh arguments should be used so that their request might be clearly and for- cibly made known. He suggested that the matter be referred to the Parliamentary and General Purposes Committee, and moved an amendment that that course be taken.--Mr. H. J. Grice seconded the amendment.— Dr. Gastaldi accepted the amendment.—After Mr. Jones and Mr. Dean had spoken, the Chairman put his amend- ment as a substantive motion and it was carried. WIGOS' WORKS. Dr. Gastaldi said he would like to know whether it was within the power of the Council to ask the Shin Canal Company to compel Wiggs' works to be put in their former order. The company were put to great expense with regard to those works, and now they were nearly closed up.—The Chairman said it was a commer- cial question. No company could force another to work at a loss.

LAT-ET ACCOMMODATION AT RUNCORN. Mr. Bisbrown suggested that a communication should be sent to the Ship Canal Company asking them to push forward more expeditiously the extension of the lay-by at Runcorn. There was a number of vessels in the canal between Eastham and Runcorn, and there was only convenience for three at the lay-by. That meant a loss to the workingmen and others at Runcorn. He pro- posed a letter be sent to the company.—The Chairman said the motion was out of order.—Mr. Wiswall said there was a delay in the settling of the agreement, but the work had now been let and sufficient time had not elapsed to complete it. The fact that the company re- quired the lay-by in its own interests for discharging vessels was sufficient to satisfy the Council that no time would be lost in its construction.—Mr. Bisbrown hoped there would be an early meeting of their Ship Canal Committee.—Mr. Hewitt was of the opinion that the work was being pushed forward by the Canal Company. —The Chairman said the Canal Company had very liberally paid the expenses or the deputation. The meeting then terminated.

The loss a £6l us. 83. on the year had consequently reduced the balance in hand from £377 Bs. 3d. to £315 18s. 91.
